seam: The archive's most persistent theme is not a policy fight but a self-doubt: from the Herald editorial "We Do Not Deserve Student Government" printed the same week Jim Haynes won the first presidency in May 1966, to the "For the People" delegation telling the senate in March 2024 that SGA had a disconnect with cultural communities, sixty years of WKU student government has been arguing about whether anyone is listening. The founding referendum of 26 April 1966 drew 2,538 voters - the archive itself notes this was "a larger raw turnout than most SGA elections have managed since" - and the organisation has spent six decades measuring itself against that number, inventing Anti-Apathy Weeks, phone banks, syllabus clauses, Uber vouchers and a "POLLapalooza" to close the gap. The record's own verdict comes from the 2026 entry: turnout tracks whether there is an actual contest.

patterns.name: The turnout numbers in sequence
patterns.what_it_is: Every vote count, percentage and ballot total the archive records, from the 1966 ratification referendum to the 2026 election, read as one series. The pattern is a very high founding number, a long stretch where the archive records almost no counts at all, and then - from 1999, when the Herald began printing office-by-office totals - a continuous series oscillating roughly between 900 and 2,400.
patterns.how_it_changed: Raw turnout has never again reached the 2,538 of the founding referendum or the 2,894 of the 1968 election (34 percent of an 8,500-student enrollment), even though enrollment more than doubled. The 2004 constitution made every enrolled student a member of SGA with the right to vote in its elections; the modern ceiling is about 2,400 voters against enrollment reported at 17,500 in 2002 and about 18,000 in 2004. Voting moved from paper polls to TopNet online balloting by the 2000s, and the counts became precise without becoming larger.

instances.what: 26 April: students ratify the constitution 1,812 to 726 in a four-day referendum. 2,538 voted - the archive notes this was a larger raw turnout than most SGA elections have managed since.

2 May: total turnout 2,894 votes, about 34 percent of the roughly 8,500-student enrollment. Straeffer beat Whitley 1,732 to 1,098; Gilpin beat Van Corbach 1,516 to 1,206; Paul Gerard took the junior class presidency 461 to 277. The internal results memo says: 'Total number of voters was 2,894 - approximately 34 percent of 8,500.'
2 March: twenty student government offices 'going begging' for candidates at filing. By 26 March the field had filled: 84 students seeking campus offices.
2 April: 527 ballots cast in the presidential primary - 'Bruce Smith, Christy Vogt Survive as 527 Cast Ballots.'
15 April: Bob Moore elected by a 26-vote margin over Tom Blair, one of the narrowest presidential margins in the record.

31 October: about 20 votes separated the top two finishers in a fall ASG election.

12 April: candidates withdrew from the ASG races, saving a primary that would otherwise have been invalid; only two candidates were running for president.

11 April: Sears beat Stinson 1,284 to 594. Bradley beat Lockhart 1,065 to 730, Pruitt ran unopposed with 1,524, Coats edged Skidmore 933 to 809, Copeland beat Johnson 1,106 to 761.

Spring turnout was 1,376, per the Herald's later comparison. 25 October: an SGA-run online referendum tied to the homecoming queen election drew 2,136 voters; 1,695 answered the Division I-A football question, about 9 percent of enrollment, backing the move 1,095 to 600.

Spring turnout was 1,424, per the Herald's later comparison. 1 February: Jeanne Johnson won the special student regent election with 688 votes, 41 percent of ballots cast. 2 October: an SGA mock gubernatorial election drew 127 student voters.

25-26 February: 701 students voted in the special student regent election; Gilley beat Eaton 477 to 224.

13-15 April: Robinson elected unopposed on a turnout of 966. The DEI-committee constitutional amendment was ratified with 88 percent in favour, and 31 senators were named.

patterns.name: Where turnout jumped, and what caused it
patterns.what_it_is: The five or six upward spikes in the series, and the reason the archive gives for each. Every one is attached either to a real contest, a referendum on the ballot, or a fight the campus was already having.
patterns.how_it_changed: The causes shift from constitutional moments (1966, 1968) to piggybacked referendums (2003, 2006) to genuinely competitive presidential races (2016, 2018, 2026). The single largest documented driver is simply whether more than one ticket is running.

instances.what: The peak of the whole record, 2,538, was the vote to create the organisation at all - a four-day referendum on the constitution, not an election of officers.

2,894 votes, 34 percent, in the organisation's second contested presidential race, with contests all the way down the ballot to secretary, treasurer and congressman at large. The Herald still ran 'Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference' in the same issue.

2,014 voted with the first student referendum in SGA history on the ballot, the $3 Revolution 91.7 fee. Executive vice president John Bradley, who championed the measure, had explicitly argued it 'would empower students and boost voter turnout' - and the presidency itself was uncontested.

2,136 voted in the I-A football referendum, which SGA deliberately ran alongside the homecoming queen election. President Rob Watkins conceded the homecoming tie-in likely drew football-friendly voters.

2,442 voters, one of the highest turnouts in the association's history, in Richey's contested re-election - the year of the Confucius Institute vote, the pub-name override and the 'impeach Ransdell' censure fight, when SGA had been unusually visible.
2,447 votes overall in a genuine three-way race decided 35-33-32 percent, with the Judicial Council disqualifying two campaigns mid-election over a Pepe the Frog meme.
Fall turnout doubled from 398 to 805 - the archive records the doubling without giving a cause.

1,601 votes, up 66 percent on 966, in the first contested presidential race in four years. Two tickets, a DSU town hall with 27 student-submitted questions, and a Herald/Revolution Radio debate preceded it.
The counterexample: turnout fell to 908, down 555 votes, in a year the sitting president had herself run unopposed and spent nothing on her campaign.

patterns.name: Uncontested races and candidate shortages
patterns.what_it_is: Presidencies and whole ballots with no opposition, and the recurring failure to find enough candidates to fill seats.
patterns.how_it_changed: The problem migrates. In the 1970s and 1980s it is offices 'going begging' at filing time and primaries cancelled for lack of candidates. In the 2000s and 2010s it is executive tickets running unopposed while senate seats go to anyone who files. By the 2020s the presidency itself is uncontested three years running - 2023, 2024, 2025 - before the 2026 contest.

instances.what: 11 April: Alana White reported that filing for Associated Student Government offices had turned up few candidates, in the same issue as a piece urging that criteria for the offices be voiced.
13 March: 'John Lyne wins the presidency before the race begins.' No opponent filed.
2 March: twenty student government offices going begging for candidates.
21 March: the ASG primary election was cancelled.
6 April: students voted in the ASG elections with four offices uncontested.

ASG races faced a candidate shortage; Bill Fogle said he had entered the presidential race to help Tim Todd rather than to win it. On election day the Herald indexed the race itself under the headline 'no contest.'
Only two of 32 congress positions were contested.
12 April: candidates withdrew to save a primary that would otherwise have been invalid; only two were running for president.
7 April: the primary was cancelled outright, too few candidates to require one.
Adam Howard and Leslie McClard ran unopposed for two of the four vice presidencies.
Bedo's ticket stood unopposed for the top job; only the public relations vice presidency had two names on it.
Bradley ran unopposed for president, winning with 1,662 of 2,014 votes cast.

September: at the interest meeting for the special election, Patti Johnson was the only student to show interest in the presidency. She said she was disappointed that students would not 'really get to make a decision.' About 13 students attended the meeting.
All 25 senate candidates on the March ballot ran unopposed and were elected; two vice presidencies were uncontested.
Both vice presidents re-elected unopposed - the Herald ran a story headlined 'Uncontested elections don't concern SGA' - and all 35 senate candidates elected to 36 seats, each needing one vote.
Both vice-presidential races uncontested.
Nicki Seay ran unopposed for administrative vice president; most college senate seats went to unopposed candidates in the fall.
Nicki Taylor ran unopposed for president and, she said, did not spend a cent.
31 March: only 13 people were running for senate, President Edmonds warned.
19 April: the entire Kurtz-Finch-León ticket ran unopposed.
11 April: at the Executive Town Hall all three executive candidates were unopposed. 17 September: no candidate at all for the graduate senator seat.
Robinson elected unopposed; Kurtz had warned the Senate repeatedly that an unusually senior chamber made the spring election matter more than usual.

patterns.name: Quorum failures and empty seats
patterns.what_it_is: Meetings that could not be held, votes that failed for want of bodies, and senators removed or resigned for absence - the internal version of the same problem.
patterns.how_it_changed: Early instances are reported as one-off embarrassments in the Herald. From the 2000s the SGA's own minutes record quorum failures directly, and by the 2010s and 2020s the Judicial Council has a codified removal machinery for absentees, culminating in a constitutional rule requiring removal after a second censure.

instances.what: 28 February: ASG action was halted twice in one week for lack of quorum. A Herald editorial said the confusion in ASG signalled a need for change.
13 November: ASG re-endorsed dorm inspections in a session the Herald reported the government had 'nearly slept through.'
13 January: no quorum, so ASG did not meet - the first ASG item the paper carried after the winter break.

2 April: attendance fell off once campaign speeches had been heard. 9 April: a constitutional amendment was defeated because too few members turned up to vote on it. 27 October: ASG moved to get tough on absenteeism after a member lost his seat.
23 February: the organisation publicly explained its empty seats; four congress positions had been filled at a single meeting. 3 November: ASG filled half of its open congress seats.

15 April: the first speaker of the senate was elected 9-8 with 17 of 20 members present, and the result was immediately questioned because the new constitution was unclear on what quorum was required.
5 September: the year's first senate meeting was called to order with 8 of 18 senators present. 5 December: with 16 of 31 present, the senate lacked quorum and tabled Resolutions 09-06-F and 10-06-F.
1 February: SGA began the spring semester with its first full senate attendance since fall 2004.
10 November: the Judicial Council removed Senator Theodore Harden for excessive unexcused absences; he did not attend to defend himself. Attendance guidelines were posted in the SGA office window.

15 November: ten of 36 senators were called before the judicial board for excessive absences; Kevin Adams and Kevin Preston were dismissed for failing to attend their own hearings, with eight to ten absences apiece.
29 February: Kevin Adams, removed the previous semester for absences, was reappointed to the senate by the president.

6 February: five members had resigned the previous semester, leaving the legislative research and public relations chairs vacant. 13 February: an amendment that had passed was voided because the Executive Council found too few senators had attended for the vote to count. 26 February: six senate seats still open.
22 April: a $500 African Student Union reimbursement passed 12-4 with many abstaining, after a two-hour meeting that ended with fewer senators present.

21 September: Speaker Nathan Cherry told the senate eleven at-large seats should have been filled the previous spring but only ten were, leaving SGA one senator short through the whole summer. 'I failed to catch that,' Cherry said.

30 January: nine senators were forced to step down, leaving the chamber depleted with no new legislation introduced. 2 October: the senate voted 17-15 to cancel a meeting for a sorority philanthropy event, with one senator arguing the practical reason was that quorum might not be met. 19 September: the budget passed with 'all 13 senators' approving.

5 February: senators and committee chairs had quietly vacated positions since the fall; the SAVES and Sustainability chairs were both empty, and President Harris posted an open SGA application on social media to recruit.

6 November: the Judicial Council voted 7-0 to remove Malick Ibrahim, Myricle Gholston and Karisha Petty, each with at least six unexcused absences, under a constitutional provision requiring removal after a second censure. The council's minutes said senators cannot represent students they are not present to serve.

4 April: the meeting to pass the DEI-committee amendment initially lacked the 21 members needed for a two-thirds vote, so absent members were phoned onto Zoom to reach quorum. 28 January: Kurtz reported several senators had resigned over the break and Judicial Council members had graduated.

patterns.name: Apathy editorials, cartoons and columns
patterns.what_it_is: The College Heights Herald's sixty-year running commentary on whether SGA matters - the single most continuous voice in the archive on this theme, from scolding non-voters to explaining them to mocking the organisation to defending it.
patterns.how_it_changed: The register moves through distinct phases: exhortation in the 1960s ('Goof Government Needs Student Vote'), resignation in the 1970s (a 1979 piece justifying student apathy - the archive notes the paper 'had moved from scolding non-voters to explaining them'), ridicule in the 1980s and 1990s (cartoons of student government in an empty room, then in a glass box), and by the 2000s and 2010s a turn on the student body itself ('pathetic') as often as on SGA.

instances.what: May: the same Herald issue that reported Jim Haynes's win carried a skeptical editorial titled 'We Do Not Deserve Student Government.' 27 October: the paper judged ASG leaders were performing well but failing to communicate with the students they represented.

9 March: Fran Salyers argued popularity, not merit, was set to decide the election - a 'popularity bandwagon.' 12 May: the first year summed up as organization, progress and apathy. 18 May: 'Goof Government Needs Student Vote.'
9 May: 'Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference' ran in the same issue as Straeffer's win.
25 February: 'Chaos Reigns at Associated Students Meeting,' with a separate piece in the same issue arguing student interest had collapsed and the Associated Students had followed it down.
26 March: an editorial held up ASG's troubles as a cautionary example for the university's newly forming Faculty Senate.
12 April: the primary issue carried a piece justifying student apathy in ASG voting.

14 April: the Herald 'dared students to vote at all' in a sardonic election-day editorial. 13 October and 6 December: Lou Bloss editorial cartoons on ASG; Jack Smith wrote in to say the cartoon aggravated him.
8 November: an editorial cartoon on the organisation ran alongside LaMont Jones dropping out of an ASG revote.
14 February: 'Voter Apathy Can be Solved' ran with a cartoon on election apathy. 11 April: an editorial credited Jack Smith's enthusiasm with reviving interest in ASG, with a Kevin Knapp cartoon.
4 March: a piece arguing student government needed a strong leader ran the same issue McKinney withdrew from re-election. 20 March: dueling letters on whether the organisation was in trouble.
14 April: a letter calling the organisation impotent, and the race headlined 'no contest.' 29 October: an article arguing apathy was killing both ASG and the Residence Hall Association.
February: an editorial told the body it needed better ideas, not gimmicks. September: an editorial said the write-in ban showed ASG was not listening.

26 January: Rebecca Fullen's 'Peddling President' feature on Scott Whitehouse selling ASG to students. 2 February: 'Scott Whitehouse Selling Good Government' with a John Chattin cartoon drawing him as a salesman.
12 April: the Herald had already reported interest in the organisation might be lower, illustrated by a cartoon of student government in an empty room.
14 April: 'Many Students Won't Vote' ran in the same issue as Rains's win. 19 November: Paul Weathers urged students to get involved.
8 February: 'Let's Work Together for Change,' a People Poll asking how SGA could reach more students, and a Stacy Curtis cartoon offering a 'recipe for better representation.'

20 April: 'Tara Higdon Moves Up; Voting Down.' 25 April: a Stacy Curtis cartoon of student government in a glass box, paired with the editorial 'Visibility Key to Student Government Association Success.'

13 February: a letter dismissing the association as a 'puppet' group. 18 April: 'Few Turn Out for Election.' 25 April: a column headlined 'Students Just Don't Care About Student Government Association.'
28 April: election-week dueling letters on whether the association served students, and a column arguing the $15,000 electronic message sign money could be better used.
15 April: 'Student Government Association Offers No Leadership.' 20 April: an editorial cartoon on nasty campaigns and an opinion piece describing a 'swath of scandal' around the elections.
20 April: 'Student Government Association Membership Still Declining.'
24 September: the Herald's 11-member editorial board attacked SGA over 'Gazebo-Gate,' calling leaders' ignorance about the missing money 'shameful.'

16 March: an editorial criticised student participation after only 132 of about 18,000 students voted on the new constitution, contrasting it with the 86 percent who voted in South Africa's 1999 general elections.
20 April: an editorial titled 'SGA misspending' said members should not have to be 'motivated by a giveaway to show up for meetings.' December: 'SGA actions an embarrassment to Western.'
15 November: the editorial board told Stephens to drop the building renaming and keep his platform promises, noting no visible progress on Provide-a-Ride.
7 February: after two short meetings and no new plans on the agenda, an editorial said SGA appeared not to be on the ball.
5 November: an editorial said SGA had one job, representing students, and had not done it on the priority-registration cap.
15 April: the editorial reporting turnout of 908 called turnout below 1,000 pathetic and said the student body could and should do better.

29 March: the student advocacy group 'For the People' told the Senate SGA was the only major organisation not to oppose Turning Point USA bringing Kyle Rittenhouse to campus, said 40 percent of the Senate belonged to Greek life, and said SGA had a disconnect with cultural communities on campus.

patterns.name: What SGA tried in order to fix it
patterns.what_it_is: Sixty years of counter-measures: surveys, self-evaluations, structural seats, outreach campaigns, incentives and giveaways aimed at making students notice, vote and run.
patterns.how_it_changed: The tools evolve from communication (surveys, phone banks, forums) to structural representation (new seats for colleges, regional campuses, international, first-generation, transfer and Honors students) to marketing and material incentives (extra credit for attending a debate, Uber vouchers, raffles, a syllabus clause). Two moves cut in opposite directions on the same problem: in 2017 the senate lowered SGA's own GPA requirement from 2.5 to 2.0 to make the body more representative, ratified by referendum; in March 2024 senators voted amendments raising the floors back to 2.5 for senate and 2.75 for cabinet.

instances.what: 8 December: the Associated Students published a survey of what activities students wanted, reported alongside a letter commending the government's efforts.
19 September: ASG 'corrected a tactical error by adding more polls to a campus vote.'
Taking office, Jeff Consolo told the Herald he hoped for increased student involvement during his term. 22 February: ASG voted to retain its campaign spending limit rather than loosen the cap.
28 March: ASG passed a motion simplifying voting procedures for the spring election.
15 February: Bill 6 proposed that ASG conduct a self-evaluation 'for the purposes of transparency and improvement.' 12 April: outgoing president Christy Vogt wrote 'Urges Involvement' for the Herald.
9 March: spending limits set for the coming election. 7 September: ASG decided its roll-call votes would be made public.
21 February: ASG considered changing the date of its spring elections.

11 September: ASG planned to reach students by telephone to collect their ideas and needs, alongside a $12,100 budget and a retreat with President Kern Alexander. 18 September: a minor change in voting procedures. 25 March: major/minor college representative seats created. 1 April: a revised SGA membership application process adopted.

15 September: write-in campaigns banned after write-in votes threw the presidential election into dispute. 29 September: the organisation reported working to make the importance of voting register with students.

15 February: Anti-Apathy Week announced; it drew enough criticism that President Amos Gott wrote a defence of it in the paper a week later. 29 March: the congress voted to expand itself so classes and student groups had more voice. 19 April: ASG asked for the student activity fee to be raised.
January: SGA adopted written 'Guidelines for SGA Public Forums,' formalising a process that had previously run ad hoc.
7 September: 'Tara Higdon Seeks Student Interest in Group.'

15 September: Bill 99-10-F created an SGA Information Technology Director, with a companion bill amending the constitution to include website guidelines. 2 November: Resolution 99-4-F proposed Topline, a toll-free campus activity phone line.
17 February: SGA proposed a rewrite of its election codes to close loopholes, followed by debate over fairness between candidates and campaign spending limits.

19 August: an SGA Ambassador Council created to visit student organisations weekly. 4 March: the $3 radio-fee referendum placed on the ballot expressly to 'empower students and boost voter turnout.' 30 October: the senate suspended its bylaws to pass a resolution urging students to vote in the 4 November state election.

The Constitutional Convention rebuilt the body into three branches, and, in what the archive calls the most consequential and quietest clause, made every enrolled student a member of SGA with the right to vote in its elections.

Record interest reported in the fall senate election, 25 candidates for 20 seats, 'the most applications President Jeanne Johnson said she had ever seen.' SGA also co-sponsored a mock gubernatorial election.

Defending the one-week campaign window, Johnson pointed to new turnout efforts her administration tried: holding the debate during SGA week, arranging extra credit for students who attended it, and adding candidate profiles and questionnaires to the SGA website.

August: Stephens opened with a revamped PR campaign built around asking students what SGA could do for them, aimed at raising fall election turnout, producing contested races and filling all 36 senate seats. 'I want PR to be visible on campus.'

12 September: a constitutional amendment created a Navitas/ESL international student senate seat, which Boka said would make WKU the first student government in the state with one. 26 February: amendments replaced class-year seats with college-based representation and guaranteed seats for the Glasgow and Owensboro regional campuses.
MyCampusToo launched as Richey's campaign initiative to bring underrepresented students into SGA, alongside listening tours of the Glasgow, Owensboro and Elizabethtown/Fort Knox campuses.

16 November: SafeWalk launched and SGA extended office hours so students had a place to go; the Sustainability and MyCampusToo committees were made permanent, MyCampusToo renamed the Committee for Diversity and Inclusion. Richey also told senators appointments should be more democratic, noting he had appointed 42 percent of the sitting senate.

15 February: non-voting regional ambassador positions created for each regional campus, a South Campus liaison designated, and every senator required to keep one office hour a week - Speaker Nathan Cherry said it would make senators feel more connected and more willing to write legislation. 5 April: the GPA requirement lowered from 2.5 to 2.0 by exactly the 24 votes needed, to make the body more representative; ratified by student referendum on 19 April.

Edmonds campaigned on creating a Director of Outreach to close the communication gap between campus organisations and SGA; an ad hoc outreach committee chaired by Me'Lon Craighead was formed that October.
11 February: a bill funded 50 laminated, QR-coded outreach signs for campus.

16 February: Resolution 6-22-S added an SGA clause to course syllabi listing meeting times, office location and the organisation's purpose - reported as the first of its kind in SGA history. 5 October: Bornefeld, Reed and Kurtz reported holding a campus listening tour to increase SGA's accessibility.

15 February: 450 Uber vouchers worth $10 each, distributed through social media giveaways, meeting attendance and SGA events. 29 March: senators voted on 13 constitutional amendments, including raising senate and cabinet GPA floors back to 2.5 and 2.75.

26 February: Kurtz announced POLLapalooza, telling the Senate 'My goal is that 3,000 students vote in our election' - the eventual turnout was 966. 24 September: a bill replaced the Hilltoppers concern form, which author Jakob Barker said was buried behind five links on WKU's homepage, with a pop-up, and a second bill funded a raffle giveaway to build SGA's social media following.

24 March: SGA used its projects fund for a baseball tailgate with free hot dogs, giveaways and a scholarship drawing, answering Athletics Director Todd Stewart's call for more student engagement at games.

patterns.name: Where the archive is thin
patterns.what_it_is: The decades in which the theme is documented only by headlines and adjectives, with no numbers behind them. These gaps are not neutral - they mean the turnout series cannot be read as a smooth curve.
patterns.how_it_changed: Documentation improves in three steps: the Herald index (headlines only) for the 1970s and 1980s; full Herald text with office-by-office vote totals from 1999; and SGA's own posted minutes and constitutions from the mid-2000s. The best-documented apathy material is therefore the most recent, which risks making the modern era look worse than it is.

instances.what: No general-election turnout figure survives for any year in this stretch. The 1972 constitutional referendum is explicit: 'The archive does not yet show the referendum's result or turnout.'

The decade yields only three raw counts - 527 ballots in the 1976 primary, 95 in the 1978 freshman primary, 830 in the 1979 primary - plus a 26-vote margin in 1977. There is not one general-election total for the entire decade.

Explicitly flagged: 'The archive does not yet show what Hargrove's administration passed or fought over during 1979-80... Further Herald issues from the fall and spring semester have not yet been checked.'
Only primary figures (about 500 in 1983, about 450 in 1984) and a 20-vote margin in 1985. For 1987 even the result is missing: 'The indexed issues that survive do not record the published result.'
One number in nine years - 'about 1,200' in April 1992. The 1995 and 1996 headlines ('Tara Higdon Moves Up; Voting Down'; 'Few Turn Out for Election') describe a decline the archive cannot quantify.
For the Bedo unopposed ticket: 'no results or turnout figures were found in allowed sources.'
'The Herald's results story reported no turnout figures.' The only figure is Edmonds's own September estimate of about 1,500, offered while calling turnout 'awful.'

No presidential turnout figures for either the September 2020 Edmonds-Mayo election or the April 2021 Wininger election. The 398-vote fall 2021 figure survives only because the 2022 story compared against it.
Even at the end, one Herald story on the Lucas win 'did not publish vote totals or turnout figures'; the 1,601 count comes from a separate entry.

notes:
Source: /Users/samkurtz/Downloads/sga60/data/years.json, read in full - all 61 year records (1966-67 through 2026-27), including every leader note and profile paragraph, every event body, and the organization, documents and status fields. Nothing outside this file was used.

Method note: the file frequently carries the same event twice, once in a short summary form and once in a longer form (for example the 2011 fall election appears as both '977 votes cast' entries, and the 2016 Richey re-election appears twice). I have merged duplicates rather than counting them as separate instances.

Three cautions on reading the sequence as a trend line:
1. The denominators change. The only turnout percentage in the whole archive is 1968's 34 percent of about 8,500 students. Enrollment figures appear only sporadically afterwards - 14,543 in 1997, about 17,770 and 17,500 in 2002, about 18,000 in 2004 - so the modern raw counts of 900 to 2,400 cannot be converted to comparable percentages except at those points. The one modern percentage the archive does give is from the 2006 football referendum: the 1,695 students who answered the question were about 9 percent of enrollment.
2. Fall senate elections and spring executive elections are different animals and should not be compared directly. Fall totals in the record run 398 to 977; spring totals run 908 to 2,447.
3. Some numbers in the file are presidential-race votes and some are total ballots cast. Where both exist for one election (2016: 2,442 voters, 2,341 presidential votes; 2018: 2,447 overall, 2,378 presidential) I have given both.

Two internally inconsistent figures worth flagging: the 2014 Herald editorial says turnout of 908 was 'down 555 votes from the year before,' implying 1,463 in 2013, but the 2013 presidential race totals given elsewhere in the same file (626 + 419 + 300) come to 1,345. And the 2000-01 gazebo money is described as about $5,000 in one entry and $13,000 in another. Both are the archive's own numbers, reported as found.

I did not treat the plaque-year disputes, name spellings or the student regent seat's history as part of this theme except where they bear directly on it - for instance the February 2009 special regent election (701 votes) and the February 2007 special regent election (688 votes, 41 percent of ballots cast), which are among the few hard turnout figures for off-cycle votes.

seam: The Herald is the seam, and it opens with a verdict rather than a welcome: the same May 1966 issue that reported Jim Haynes elected first president of the Associated Students carried an editorial headed "We Do Not Deserve Student Government." Sixty years of commentary in this archive are variations on that sentence. The dominant charge is never corruption and rarely policy - it is irrelevance. Apathy is named as the organisation's disease in 1967 ("organization, progress and apathy"), is still the disease in 1987 ("apathy is killing ASG"), and is still being measured in 2014 ("pathetic"). What changes is the register. From 1966 to about 1980 the paper scolds the student body for not deserving its government. From 1980 to 1999 it stops arguing and starts drawing: fourteen editorial cartoons in this record, from a cockroach in 1980 to Heather Falmlen as a ventriloquist's dummy and Joe Rains as Darth Vader in 1992, and the presidents write back in the letters column. After 1999 the cartoons stop entirely in this archive and the criticism migrates from the opinion page into the room itself - to students standing up at meetings, to organisations withdrawing recognition, to censure hearings, Title IX complaints and a federal lawsuit. The last two decades' harshest verdicts on SGA are delivered by SGA members about each other, and the harshest quotes in the whole file ("almost toxic in nature," "absolute hell") come from a sitting president and vice president describing their own year.

patterns.name: "We do not deserve student government" - the founding verdict of unworthiness
patterns.what_it_is: The Herald doubted the organisation's right to exist from the week it was created, and the doubt was recycled as a standing editorial frame for two decades. This is the oldest and most quoted line in the archive.
patterns.how_it_changed: Framed in 1966-72 as a judgement on the student body ('we do not deserve'); by the mid-1970s and 1980s recast as a judgement on the organisation itself; by 1987 the language is simply 'impotent'.

instances.what: The Herald ran the editorial 'We Do Not Deserve Student Government' in the same issue that reported Jim Haynes's election as the first president of the Associated Students.
Midway through the first fall the Herald judged leaders performing well but failing to communicate with the students they represented - the first public report card on the year-old government.
Reviewing the government's first year the Herald found 'organization, progress and apathy'; the same issue carried a letter arguing the Associated Students really worked.
Bill Martin's column questioned the Judicial Council's work; a letter in an earlier issue was headed 'Wanted: Work for Judicial Council'.
As Menser's term ended the Herald ran 'Past Performance of Associated Student Government Analyzed' - the archive holds the headline only, not the text.
'Chaos Reigns at Associated Students Meeting', alongside a separate piece arguing student interest had collapsed and the Associated Students had followed it down.
An editorial held up the Associated Student Government's troubles as a cautionary example for the university's newly forming Faculty Senate.
On election day the Herald endorsed the challenger, printed a letter calling the organisation impotent, and headlined the race itself 'no contest'.

patterns.name: Apathy, named and re-named for six decades
patterns.what_it_is: The single most persistent charge. Apathy is diagnosed in editorials, drawn in cartoons, made into a candidate's platform, and eventually turned into an SGA-branded event.
patterns.how_it_changed: 1967-1978 the paper scolds non-voters; by April 1979 it prints a piece justifying student apathy - it has moved from scolding non-voters to explaining them; by 1972 and 1990 SGA has co-opted the word ('anti-apathy', Anti-Apathy Week); after 2003 apathy is discussed as a turnout statistic rather than a moral failing.

instances.what: The Herald ran 'Goof Government Needs Student Vote', pressing students toward greater turnout as Menser's administration took over.
The issue reporting Bill Straeffer's win carried the editorial 'Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference'; turnout was 2,894 votes, about 34 percent of 8,500 students.
The Herald profiled ASG vice president Michael Fiorella under a headline calling him anti-apathy, a week before he won the student regent seat.
830 students voted in the spring primary and the same issue carried a piece justifying student apathy in ASG voting.
David Payne's first appearance in the indexed record is a Herald letter titled 'Apathy Erased', a year before he became president.
'Voter Apathy Can be Solved' ran alongside a cartoon on election apathy and a report on the 24-hour open house debate.
The Herald ran an article arguing that apathy was killing both Associated Student Government and the Residence Hall Association.
ASG's Anti-Apathy Week drew enough criticism that president Amos Gott wrote a defence of it in the paper a week later.
The issue reporting the swearing-in of new officers carried the column 'Students Just Don't Care About Student Government Association'.
President-elect John Bradley called the year's high election turnout the semester's best moment and pledged to fight student apathy the next year.
A Herald editorial criticised student participation after only 132 of about 18,000 students voted on the new constitution, contrasting it with 86 percent turnout in South Africa's 1999 election.
An editorial reported spring turnout of 908, down 555 votes on the year before, and called turnout below 1,000 pathetic.

patterns.name: Candidate shortages and elections nobody contested
patterns.what_it_is: Recurring news stories about offices going begging, uncontested ballots, cancelled primaries and candidates who entered races without meaning to win. The archive's own closing observation is that turnout tracks whether a contest exists.
patterns.how_it_changed: In the 1960s-70s the shortage is reported as a scandal ('twenty offices go begging'); by the 2000s-2020s it is reported flatly as routine, with unopposed presidential tickets in 2001, 2023 and 2024 drawing no editorial at all.

instances.what: Alana White reported that filing for Associated Student Government offices turned up few candidates, in the same issue as a piece urging that criteria for the offices be voiced.
With filing open, the Herald reported twenty student government offices going begging for candidates; by election eve 84 students had filed for campus offices.
Steve Thornton and Ed Johnson contested the presidency while four other offices had no opponent on the ballot.
A candidate shortage across the races, with Bill Fogle saying he had entered the presidential race to help Tim Todd rather than to win it.
Scott Whitehouse emerged from a field of seven for president in a year when only two of 32 congress positions were contested.
Candidate withdrawals saved a primary that would otherwise have been invalid; only two candidates were running for president.
The ASG primary was cancelled outright, with too few candidates to require one.
SGA's own candidate page listed a single ticket for the top job, Leslie Bedo with Jamie Sears; only the public relations vice presidency had two names.
About 13 students attended the special-election interest meeting and Patti Johnson was the only student to show interest in the presidency.
All 35 senate candidates were elected to the 36 open seats, each needing just one vote to win.
President Garrett Edmonds warned senators that only 13 people were running for senate in the April election.
Sam Kurtz was elected on a ticket that ran unopposed, and was re-elected unopposed again in 2024 on a ballot of more than 60 legislative candidates.
Chief Justice Ellen Henderson reported 20 students running for freshman senator, one each for Gatton and international, and none for the graduate seat.
A contested race drew 1,601 voters, 635 more than the year before - the archive calls it the clearest evidence that WKU turnout tracks whether there is an actual contest.

patterns.name: The cartoons: drawing the presidents, 1980-1999
patterns.what_it_is: For two decades the Herald's sharpest commentary on SGA was pictorial. Fourteen editorial cartoons appear in the record, several naming a sitting president as their subject, and at least one president wrote in to protest.
patterns.how_it_changed: Cartoons begin in 1980 with policy mockery (a cockroach), move by 1989-1992 to caricaturing named presidents (salesman, ventriloquist's dummy, Darth Vader), and by 1990-1995 to images of emptiness and isolation (an empty room, a glass box). No editorial cartoon about SGA appears anywhere in this archive after 1999.

instances.what: ASG's bill calling for a ban on bugs in the dorms drew a cartoon depicting a cockroach imperiled by the resolution.
A Lou Bloss cartoon on an ASG penalty ran in the same issue as ASG's request for cable television in dorm rooms.
ASG voided its own procedures; the editorial page mocked the body with a cartoon and president Jack Smith wrote in under the heading 'Cartoon Aggravates'.
LaMont Jones withdrew from an ASG revote and the same issue carried an editorial cartoon on the organisation.
A cartoon on election apathy ran with the 'Voter Apathy Can be Solved' piece.
Kevin Knapp drew an editorial cartoon on Jack Smith and the organisation in the issue marking the end of his presidency.
John Chattin drew Scott Whitehouse as a salesman, alongside the piece 'Scott Whitehouse Selling Good Government'; the Herald had called him the 'Peddling President' the week before.
During ASG's fight for weekend service from the Unicorn pizza vendor, a cartoon showed ASG and the administration riding a unicorn.
A report that interest in the organisation might be lower was illustrated with a cartoon of student government in an empty room.
Patrick Richardson's cartoon 'Ventriloquist's Dummy' took president Heather Falmlen as its subject, in the issue reporting SGA's plan for a student regent committee.
On election day Richardson drew Joe Rains as Darth Vader, running against a letter headed 'Associated Student Government Needs Joe Rains'.
Stacy Curtis drew a 'recipe for better representation', paired with the piece 'Let's Work Together for Change' and a People Poll on reaching more students.
Stacy Curtis drew student government in a glass box, paired with the editorial 'Visibility Key to Student Government Association Success'.
A cartoon on nasty campaigns ran with the report that SGA's Judicial Council had overturned the spring election and an opinion piece describing a 'swath of scandal'.

patterns.name: Presidents answering back in print
patterns.what_it_is: A distinct sub-genre: the sitting or outgoing president using the Herald's own pages to correct, dispute or defend against its coverage. It runs from 1972 to 2015 and is one of the few places the archive preserves an officer's own voice.
patterns.how_it_changed: Early replies are corrections of fact (1972, 1977); by the 1980s they are complaints about tone and cartoons; by the late 1990s the reply becomes documentary - circulating the legislative record itself as rebuttal; after 2001 presidents publish self-criticism rather than defence.

instances.what: President Linda Jones wrote a piece headlined 'Associated Students Corrects Herald', a public correction of the paper's reporting on the organisation.
Stung by election-season criticism, president Steve Yater defended his administration in a letter; two weeks later the paper ran dueling letters headed 'Linda Jones vs. Steven Yater'.
After the editorial 'Bob Moore's Comment Isn't Good Politics', Moore wrote back disputing it, in the issue that named David Bass vice president.
Reader Luis Dickson published a letter taking issue with a Herald editorial about ASG, mid-campaign season.
Days after a sharply critical opinion piece said Tim Todd lacked knowledge of his own issues, Todd answered in print criticising the paper's reporting.
Amos Gott published a defence of Anti-Apathy Week after it drew criticism, in the same issue as ASG's Pearce-Ford Tower windows demand.
Future president Kristen Miller's piece 'Student Government Association Defends Itself' ran alongside letters defending the organisation in the election wrap-up issue.

Vice president Matthew Bastin circulated a memo listing the fall's passed legislation to the adviser, officers, committee heads and the Herald's editor, answering accusations of unproductiveness - the list itself was the rebuttal.
President Leslie Bedo's own op-ed, 'Meeting Goals of Student Government Association, But Not Students'', was answered in the same issue by member Troy Ransdell's 'Action, Not Complaints'.
Jay Todd Richey wrote to the Herald over the Confucius Institute vote, rejecting warnings that it made 'powerful enemies' and saying accountability and transparency should be top priorities.

patterns.name: The editorial verdict: from scolding to contempt, with intervals of praise
patterns.what_it_is: Straight editorial judgement on the organisation's competence, distinct from apathy commentary. The archive preserves both the beatings and the occasional endorsement, usually in the same decade.
patterns.how_it_changed: 1975-1988 the tone is corrective ('needs change', 'better ideas, not gimmicks'), with real praise appearing in 1985 and 1988. 1996-2006 it turns openly contemptuous ('pie-in-the-sky', 'puppet', 'shameful', 'embarrassment'). After 2011 the editorials narrow to specific failures of representation rather than broad character attacks, and after 2018 editorial criticism largely disappears from this record.

instances.what: ASG action was halted twice in one week for lack of quorum; a Herald editorial said the confusion in ASG signalled a need for change.
Within two weeks of ASG announcing its goals, its executives were defending their actions and the editorial page complained that petty politics plagued the organisation.
ASG voted to study its discount card after the Herald editorialised that the organisation should govern, not market cards; the columns 'Cheap Shots' and 'And Old Tricks' followed.
The Herald marked Jack Smith's exit with a news story, a cartoon, and an editorial crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in ASG.
Days after ASG publicly explained its empty seats, an editorial told the body it needed better ideas, not gimmicks; that September another said the write-in ban showed ASG was not listening.
After ASG filled half its open seats and sought shelters for shuttle stops, the Herald editorialised that its efforts directly helped and served students.
Five days after the skywalk proposal the Herald told SGA to 'ditch' the 'pie-in-the-sky' idea, and a letter in the same issue called the association a 'puppet' group.
'Keith Coffman Served Students Well' ran with a People Poll asking students what they thought of his performance.
The turbulent spring election issue carried the opinion piece 'Student Government Association Offers No Leadership'.
The Herald's 11-member editorial board attacked leaders over 'Gazebo-Gate', calling their ignorance about the missing money 'shameful' and challenging Sears by name to 'do her job'.
An editorial headed 'SGA misspending' said members should not have to be 'motivated by a giveaway to show up for meetings'.
The week Rob Watkins resigned as president and student regent, a Herald editorial was headlined 'SGA actions an embarrassment to Western'.
The editorial board told Billy Stephens to drop the building-renaming push and keep his platform promises, noting no visible progress on Provide-A-Ride.
After two short meetings and no new plans on the agenda, an editorial said SGA appeared not to be on the ball and urged it to do more.

An editorial said SGA had one job, representing students, and had not done it on priority registration, after the executive vice president voted for the policy at University Senate without SGA debating it.
An editorial questioned whether a handpicked international senate seat, ruled unconstitutional and then revised in a six-minute emergency meeting, was the most effective way to expand representation.
An editorial argued the Judicial Council's constitutional exemptions for two candidates set a precedent letting students with no SGA experience seek the presidency and the Board of Regents seat.

patterns.name: Administrators speaking to and about SGA
patterns.what_it_is: University presidents, deans, provosts and general counsel appearing before the body, answering it, overruling it, or being rejected by it. The relationship is the most continuous thread in the archive after the Herald itself.
patterns.how_it_changed: 1966-1972 the administration creates and funds the body (Thompson approves the constitution, Keown designs its budget), and SGA alternately endorses and rejects Downing. From the 1980s onward presidents come to meetings to ask SGA for something. From 2006 the pattern is a formal written answer to SGA legislation - Ransdell replying to four resolutions by email in 2015, declining the meningitis mandate in 2016 - and by 2025 the administration is telling SGA what state law forbids it to fund.

instances.what: President Kelly Thompson approved the constitution on 1 April; that November the Herald reported student government leaders meeting him to discuss campus problems.
Dean of Students Charles Keown sent Thompson a memo proposing a student fee structure to create a budget for the new government, attaching fee models from universities across the South and Midwest.
During Strike Western!, John Lyne and Larry Zielke presented resolutions to President Dero Downing and Dean Keown; the Congress then unanimously endorsed Downing's reply to the protesters.
The Associated Student Government rejected President Downing's position on an Office of Black Affairs, one of the sharpest confrontations of the fall.
Dean Charles Keown publicly questioned ASG's constitutional revisions the week after they were approved, as filings for office swelled to 68.
ASG scheduled a retreat featuring university president Kern Alexander, reported alongside its $12,100 budget.
University president Thomas Meredith addressed an ASG meeting, in the same issue that called Scott Whitehouse the 'Peddling President'.

Meredith came to the October congress meeting to talk about computers, laundry, cable television, lighting and Potter Hall; he returned in February 1993 to pitch Potter Hall as a student service centre.
Dean of Student Life Howard Bailey publicly contradicted Nick Todd, saying he had been sanctioned by judicial affairs in July over alleged misuse of university funds.
President Gary Ransdell came to the SGA meeting and urged senators to pass a resolution supporting the proposed $45 construction fee before the regents voted.
Ransdell said he could not condone students walking out of class for SGA's Walk Out Western protest and doubted a single-campus protest would affect state funding.
In his first visit of the semester Ransdell told senators that eliminating the two-year on-campus housing requirement did not work 'from a business standpoint'.
Ransdell said approving even a $4 student legal services fee would be difficult; weeks later he emailed faculty and staff his official response to four SGA resolutions.

Ransdell declined SGA's meningitis vaccination mandate, writing that WKU would highly recommend vaccination but 'stop short of requiring it'; that January administrators had already overridden the students' chosen pub name and Richey said he was 'very disappointed'.
Ransdell stated within days that SGA's reparations resolution, passed 19-10-1, was not a university position.
Associate Provost Rob Hale rebuffed SGA's Pass/D/Fail request; Edmonds said he was 'deeply disturbed', and after a petition of more than 3,500 signatures the university relented in December.
Title IX coordinator Deborah Wilkins opened an SGA meeting by reviewing previous SGA legislation that potentially violated Title IX.

At the Board of Regents retreat, student regent Sam Kurtz challenged administrators over student worker funding, asking the room 'to look out for the students?' and afterwards calling the answers cookie-cutter.
General Counsel Andrea Anderson told the Senate that House Bill 4 binds SGA's spending because SGA receives university money, and that the WKU Pride Center would lose its DSU office.

patterns.name: Faculty senate and university senate interactions
patterns.what_it_is: Formal contact between the student body's government and the faculty's - warnings, commendations, joint fights over grading, and mutual endorsement of each other's resolutions.
patterns.how_it_changed: The relationship starts (1976) with the Herald warning the brand-new Faculty Senate away from ASG's example. It becomes adversarial-collaborative over grading policy from 2003 to 2013. By 2017-2025 the two bodies mirror each other's resolutions deliberately, and in 2025 the Faculty Senate formally endorses two SGA resolutions.

instances.what: An editorial in the issue that opened impeachment hearings against a congress member held up ASG's troubles as a cautionary example for the university's newly forming Faculty Senate.
The WKU University Senate adopted Resolution R92.11 commending SGA president Joe Rains for joining a Frankfort rally against higher-education cuts.

SGA unanimously passed legislation against the plus/minus grading system economics professor Brian Strow proposed to the University Senate, and its petition passed 1,500 signatures as the senate voted.
Provost Barbara Burch told the University Senate she would not implement the plus/minus system it had passed 36-23; president Jeanne Johnson credited SGA's awareness campaign and student protests.
Provost Gordon Emslie pitched value-added grading to SGA, saying the earlier plus-minus proposal had taken years to develop 'only to be dashed at the last minute'.

Emslie dropped his bi-term proposal, citing student and faculty input, after both SGA and the University Senate passed resolutions against it; SGA's TA evaluation resolution went on to the Board of Regents.
Emslie and University Registrar Freida Eggleton took questions at SGA's open forum on priority registration, a policy the Herald said SGA had failed to contest in time.

SGA passed a resolution mirroring a concurrent Faculty Senate resolution urging that faculty raises be prioritised over construction, citing WKU's second-to-last pay ranking among 19 benchmarks and 57 percent of faculty rating morale poor.

After Dean Larry Snyder's forced resignation, the University Senate cast an unprecedented no-confidence vote in Provost Terry Ballman; SGA passed its own transparency resolution 30-2 demanding explanations for major decisions.
The Faculty Senate voted 40-9 for the pass-grade option SGA had campaigned for, with SGA presenting nearly 20 pages of student testimony.
The Legislative Operations Committee corrected SGA's own governing documents, which still referred to a 'University Senate' that had since split into separate Faculty and Staff senates.
The Faculty Senate voted to endorse SGA's Gordon Wilson Hall elevator resolution and its resolution on extended library hours during finals week.
Sitting beside the faculty regent during a discussion of housing, Rush Robinson told the Faculty Senate to 'take a field trip' and see the state of the residence halls.

patterns.name: Students confronting SGA from the floor
patterns.what_it_is: Non-members - and sometimes members' own constituents - coming to meetings and forums to tell the organisation it had failed them. This is the criticism that gets most concrete in the later decades, because the Herald began covering meetings weekly.
patterns.how_it_changed: Almost absent before 2000 (one 1974 protest, one 1998 anonymous letter). From 2012 it becomes routine and is the archive's main channel for criticism after the editorial cartoons stop: petitions, testimony about disability and racism, and organised advocacy groups reading SGA its own demographics.

instances.what: Protesters urged a revamping of the Associated Student Government, in the same issue that reported ASG's ecology projects were non-existent.
An anonymous congress member wrote to the Executive Council about the tone and mood of SGA meetings; Mitchell Bailey issued a written response a week later.
Members Brooke Smith, Dana Lockhart and Sam Stinson petitioned congress over $28,000 they said was unaccounted for; president Jamie Sears said 'I have absolutely no idea where that money went'.
Students who were not SGA members attended the final meeting of the year specifically to watch the vote on the transgender and gender-nonconforming support resolution, which passed 18-5.
Sophomore Nick Conrad gathered more than 700 signatures in about a week for 24-hour campus dining and brought the petition to SGA representatives.
Covington senior Logan Eckler went before SGA after days on crutches to ask for benches at campus bus stops, saying the same problem affected pregnant students and people with disabilities.

At the South Campus open forum, senators debated the lack of communication over the campus store's closing; the executive vice president said the same had happened the previous year when the food court closed.

Students Cheyenne Mitchell, Francisco Serrano, Jeb Veeck and Spencer Wells addressed senators about racist vandalism and discrimination; sophomore Brendan Ward told them his ADHD and dyslexia had cost him merit scholarships.

LGBTQ activists addressed the senate after a senator read Bible verses to explain his vote against Lavender Graduation stoles; Queer Student Union president Jeremy McFarland had walked out during the speech.
Former senator Jay Wells urged SGA to form a labour committee, citing cut student worker hours and the CAPE committee's recommendation to suspend 101 of WKU's 380 academic programs.

Avery Wells and the advocacy group 'For the People' told the Senate SGA was the only major organisation not to oppose Turning Point USA bringing Kyle Rittenhouse to campus, called the executive board's response unacceptable, and said 40 percent of the Senate belonged to Greek life.
Wheelchair user and honorary SGA member Kiersten Washington drove the Gordon Wilson Hall elevator resolution after being scheduled for a third-floor class in a 1927 building with no elevator.

patterns.name: Withdrawal: organisations and members leaving the room
patterns.what_it_is: The strongest available criticism short of a lawsuit - resigning, breaking affiliation, or formally refusing to associate with SGA.
patterns.how_it_changed: Early withdrawals are institutional and reversible (a delegation leaves the intercollegiate legislature in 1982 and rejoins by 1985). From 2009 onward they are personal and reputational: senators and justices resigning over appointments, complaints and ridicule, and in 2023 an outside student organisation publicly withdrawing recognition of SGA as a safe space.

instances.what: ASG representative Reginald Glass resigned his post in protest, an early sign of strain inside the congress.
The Associated Student Government broke from the student legislature; by February 1984 the Kentucky Student Legislature delegation was reported possibly rejoining.
ASG considered dropping its membership in the intercollegiate legislature; an editorial the following week argued the Kentucky Intercollegiate State Legislature was worth keeping.

Senators Michel Stephens, Emmett Stephens and Daniel Shaw resigned over president Kevin Smiley's nomination to the Student Publications Committee, Michel Stephens saying the pick was not based on merit or experience.
Chief Justice Kelsey Luttrell announced she would step down, saying the Judicial Council had been publicly ridiculed and lacked support from fellow SGA members.

Senator Braxton Powell and justice John McKinney resigned the morning after a complaint of racist remarks by SGA members was aired; the planned investigation was dropped because they had already left.
Senator Chase Coffey resigned the same night the Executive Council vetoed his unanimously passed resolution as unconstitutional.
Former Public Relations Chair Will Hurst walked out, part of a year the Herald documented as escalating internal conflict.
Speaker of the Senate Nathan Terrell resigned and quit the executive vice president race after a video showing him using a racial slur was sent anonymously to the Herald.
Queer Student Union president Alistar Flowers told the senate QSU had removed SGA meetings from its list of campus safe spaces and would not associate with SGA until a public apology was released.
The Senate had to waive the constitutional requirement that chief justice candidates serve a full year as associate chief justice, because neither candidate qualified.

patterns.name: Money as the sharpest charge
patterns.what_it_is: Financial scandal produces the archive's harshest language, from both the Herald and SGA's own members. Every decade from the 1970s on has at least one.
patterns.how_it_changed: 1975-1983 the charges are aired and adjudicated internally (impeachment, acquittal, a commission scheme). 1998-2011 they are investigated by the paper and the university's internal auditor and end careers. From 2013 the criticism turns to conflict of interest and procedure rather than missing money, and is brought by officers against each other.

instances.what: Charges of ASG fund misuse were heard the same week the congress voted to create an activities committee and a letter writer attacked the organisation.
ASG opened impeachment hearings against congress member Gerard Faulk as the spring campaign began; he was acquitted in April during election week.
ASG offered its own members a commission on discount card sales, prompting the columns 'Cheap Shots' and 'And Old Tricks' and an editorial saying the body should govern, not market cards.
A letter accused SGA of wasting time and money in the same issue that reported its dorm sprinkler push and a count showing its legislative output trailing the previous year.

'Gazebo-Gate': $13,000 earmarked for a campus gazebo went back into the general fund and was spent on other things including computers for the SGA office; the finance vice president said 'I didn't do my homework'.

President-elect Nick Todd was investigated over $611 missing from an SGA Dining Dollars account; the internal auditor found $872 in questionable purchases, and he resigned in July. Former SGA officers wrote to the Herald saying they were dismayed by his lack of integrity.
SGA left about $24,000 of its $115,000 budget unspent, money that returned to WKU's general fund; the administrative vice president called it a bad budgetary year.

SGA paid Parking Services a surprise $15,000 retroactive bill for the previous year's Provide-A-Ride, taking $7,500 each from organisational aid and scholarships; Billy Stephens said he was 'shocked' while his predecessor insisted the money had been budgeted.

President Cory Dodds and three others published a commentary attacking the senate for rejecting an amendment barring serving members from SGA-sponsored scholarships, writing that 11 members had received such awards since spring 2011 and calling it a breach of student trust.

Former senator Jody Dahmer published a letter arguing a precedent set that session had damaged the organisational aid process, describing groups meeting the committee outside the senate and reports being voted on quickly.
The Judicial Council voted 6-0 to censure Administrative Vice President Salvador León for spending funds, including a $425.25 Preston Center deposit, before the Senate passed the funding bill.

patterns.name: Greek dominance as a standing complaint
patterns.what_it_is: A charge with a fifty-year arc: that fraternities and sororities control the organisation out of all proportion to their numbers. Uniquely, the archive supplies the arithmetic.
patterns.how_it_changed: Reported as an observation about elections in the 1970s ('Greek influence', 'Greeks continued to dominate'), quantified in 2011 (21 of 50 members, over 40 percent, against under 8 percent of the student body), legislated against and defeated in 2018, and thrown back at SGA by outside students in 2024 with the same 40 percent figure.

instances.what: Jeff Consolo and Steve Henry won the spring election in a cycle whose primary the Herald said showed Greek influence.
Reporting Steve Henry's election, the paper noted Greeks continued to dominate the campus political scene.
The Herald reported 21 of SGA's 50 members belonged to Greek organisations, more than 40 percent, against less than 8 percent of the student body; two fraternities accounted for nine of them.
Administrative Vice President Wade Pierce said he would be succeeded by his organisational aid co-chair and Lambda Chi Alpha 'little brother' Devon Hilderbrandt, who ran unopposed.
William Hurst objected that nominating 'another fraternity man' was hypocritical given the executive board's stated concern about Greek over-representation.

Bill 10-18-F, barring SGA funding to Interfraternity and Panhellenic chapters, failed 16-17; author Amy Wyer, herself in a sorority, cited the University of Alabama's Machine and said 'I fear we have the potential to move in this direction'.
The senate voted 17-15 to cancel a meeting for a sorority philanthropy event; two senators organised a protest at that event instead over a video of Alpha Xi Delta members singing a racial slur.

Senators questioned whether president Will Harris's status as an Alpha Xi Delta knight motivated the executive board's 4-0 veto of the resolution seeking discipline against the chapter; he rejected the charge.
The student group 'For the People' told the Senate that 40 percent of it belonged to Greek life and that SGA had a disconnect with cultural communities on campus.

patterns.name: Praise, and who was willing to give it
patterns.what_it_is: The minority report. Praise in this archive comes overwhelmingly from three sources: individual letter writers, the outgoing body commending itself, and the institution's formal resolutions - rarely from the Herald's editorial page.
patterns.how_it_changed: 1967-1973 praise is a letter defending the idea of student government at all. In the 1980s-90s it is institutional: commendation bills, Board of Regents and University Senate resolutions. After 2000 editorial praise nearly vanishes and is replaced by administrators thanking SGA for specific programs and by SGA's own ceremonies - standing ovations, a red suit jacket handed president to president.

instances.what: The December issue carrying the ASG activity survey also ran a piece by Dennis Jaffe commending the government's efforts and a letter headed 'Commends Associated Student Government's Efforts'.
The Herald ran the outgoing administration's own account of its year under 'Associated Students Produces Year of Advancement'.
An editorial by Pence and Carter argued the new ASG president needed cooperation and support to succeed; that September a congressman's letter called criticism of ASG unjustified.
A letter praising Ed Jordan ran in the Herald as voting opened for the top ASG offices.
An editorial companion to the news of Jack Smith's exit said his enthusiasm had revived student interest in ASG.
The outgoing congress passed Bill 86-13-S commending president Mitchell McKinney; that August the Board of Regents included a resolution honouring him at its meeting.
An editorial said ASG's efforts directly helped and served students, the week after it filled half its open congress seats.
The Board of Regents carried a resolution of appreciation for outgoing president and student regent Donald Smith as Robert Evans was sworn in.
An opinion piece ran under the headline 'Student Government Association Doing Good Job with Trees', crediting the association's campus planting work.
'Keith Coffman Served Students Well' ran with a People Poll on his performance in the issue that reported candidates preparing for the spring election.
A Herald profile by Molly O'Connor reported renewed interest in SGA under Leslie Bedo as her term ended.
A Board of Regents resolution thanked Jeanne Johnson for her service as student member, calling her term one of 'able leadership, faithful service, and dedication'.

Donald Smith, president in 1993-94, told the Herald that structures had changed but 'a voice for the students has remained unphased'; that same year President Caboni commended SGA for its role in creating the Big Red Backpack program.
At the 24th Senate's final meeting Sam Kurtz, Donte Reed and Ethan Taylor each received a standing ovation; Kurtz's parting words to senators were 'Please be for the students'.

patterns.name: The criticism turns inward: censure, harassment and litigation
patterns.what_it_is: From about 2017 the most serious charges against SGA come from inside it and are pursued through the organisation's own courts, WKU's conduct offices and the federal courts, not the opinion page.
patterns.how_it_changed: This is the archive's clearest tonal break. Where a 1976 impeachment ended in acquittal reported as election-season colour, the 2018-2024 cases involve Title IX offices, no-contact orders, a presidential task force and a settlement. The organisation's rules also change to match: by 2024 the constitution allows removal after two censures in a year.

instances.what: After Howard Bailey reinstated president-elect Keyana Boka over the Judicial Council's disqualification, Chief Justice Seth Church called the intervention 'a serious infringement on our autonomy'.

The Herald documented more than 15 proposed constitutional amendments against about 10 the year before, an emergency judicial meeting and a walkout; Andi Dahmer said the year 'has become almost toxic in nature' and did not seek re-election.

Dahmer described months of harassment: senators cursing at her, a GroupMe called the 'Justice Friends' wishing her harm, and a profane note on her car - 'That's when I really started fearing for my life on this campus'.
In her final officer report Executive Vice President Savannah Molyneaux called the year 'awful' and an 'absolute hell' and said sexism and misogyny persisted in the senate.
Caboni convened a faculty-staff-student committee to review WKU's Title IX, EEO and Student Conduct processes after the Herald's report; Dahmer sued WKU, Caboni and two administrators that September.
An impeachment hearing against Associate Justice Annalicia Carlson was scheduled then cancelled for want of senators; she called it a waste of resources showing 'the pettiness of the organization'.
The Sixth Circuit vacated summary judgment on Dahmer's pre-February 2018 student-on-student harassment claims; the case settled in January 2024 with WKU's insurer paying $10,000.

Speaker of the Senate Julie Mishchuk requested a censure hearing against president Cole Bornefeld over anti-transgender Instagram posts; the Judicial Council voted unanimously against censure and a Title IX report seeking his removal was filed two days later.

The Judicial Council removed three senators 7-0 for excessive absences under the rule requiring removal after a second censure, its minutes saying senators cannot represent students they are not present to serve.

notes: Gaps, stated rather than smoothed over. (1) The 1960s criticism survives mostly as headlines. The archive repeatedly notes it does not hold the article text - for 'Past Performance of Associated Student Government Analyzed' (1968), 'Menser Discusses Head Fee' (1968), Linda Jones's 'Associated Students Corrects Herald' (1972), and the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union item (1972). We know what the Herald said the pieces were about, not what they said. (2) 1979-80 is effectively empty of commentary: the leader profile states outright that the archive does not show what Hargrove's administration passed or fought over, and Herald issues from that fall and spring have not been checked. (3) 1993-94 through 2002-03 thins badly. Several entries survive only as indexed headlines and bylines with the note that full text is not available online (the 2001 Bedo/Ransdell exchange, the 2002 'renewed interest' profile). Coverage for 2000-01 and 2001-02 rests largely on archived WKU news releases and Wayback captures of SGA's own website rather than on Herald opinion, so those two years contain almost no criticism at all - an artefact of the sources, not of a calm campus. (4) No editorial cartoon about SGA appears anywhere in this archive after the 1999 'nasty campaigns' cartoon. Whether the Herald stopped drawing SGA or the digitised index stopped recording cartoons is not resolvable from this file. (5) Faculty senate contact is a hole between 1976 and 1992: the Faculty Senate was only forming in 1976, and the archive records nothing between the editorial warning it away from ASG's example and the 1992 University Senate resolution commending Joe Rains. (6) 2020-21, the COVID year, contains no editorial criticism of SGA whatsoever; the leader note itself calls it almost certainly the most unusual term in the organisation's history and says it is worth a dedicated oral history. (7) Praise is structurally under-recorded relative to criticism, because much of the pre-2003 record is a Herald headline index and the paper headlined complaints more readily than approval. (8) Two names in this material remain flagged rather than fixed by the archive itself: 'Hargroave'/'Hargrove' and 'Keyanna'/'Keyana'.

seam: Across sixty years SGA rewrote its own constitution constantly and gained almost no new power by doing it. Every structural change that actually enlarged what the organisation could do came from outside its own document — a 1968 state statute that created the student regent seat, a 1982 state bill that changed how that seat was filled, the university's decision each year on what the budget line would be, and in 2025 a state law (House Bill 4) that told SGA what it may spend money on. The internal rewrites, from the 1969-72 revision fights through the 2004 Constitutional Convention to the 2026 codified bylaws, almost always redistributed authority among students — president versus senate, senate versus Judicial Council, at-large versus college seats — rather than adding any against the administration. The one internal clause that genuinely changed the organisation's standing is the quietest in the record: the 2004 convention made every enrolled student a member of SGA with the right to vote in its elections, and 132 of roughly 18,000 students voted on the constitution that did it. The archive's own shape reinforces the point: it is dense on legislation and thin on structure for the whole 1979-1991 stretch, where the only surviving consolidated governing document is a single 1986 snapshot of twenty years of patches.

patterns.name: The name changed once in sixty years, and it took twenty-six years to do it
patterns.what_it_is: The organisation was founded as the Associated Students of Western Kentucky University and became the Student Government Association only in 1992. Between those points the name drifted informally (the Herald used 'Associated Student Government' and 'ASG' from the late 1960s on), and two earlier attempts to change the branding failed outright.
patterns.span: 1966-1992, with committee and officer renamings continuing to 2025
patterns.how_it_changed: From a founding name imposed by the drafting committee, through two failed rebranding attempts in 1980-81 and a slogan bill in 1991, to a rename ratified by student referendum in 1992 — after which the renaming energy moved down to committee and officer titles, where it has stayed.

instances.what: Constitution of the Associated Students of Western Kentucky University approved by President Kelly Thompson on 1 April; ratified by student referendum 26 April, 1,812 to 726, with 2,538 voting — 'a larger raw turnout than most SGA elections have managed since.'
'ASG proposes a title change' (30 Oct 1980). Nothing in the archive shows it taking effect. In April 1981 a resolution asked for a new ASG logo and the congress voted to keep the present logo.
Bill #91-11-F proposed changing the organisation's slogan, in the same fall the body renamed itself.

On 7 April 1992 the Associated Students voted to rename itself the Student Government Association; students ratified it by referendum on 14 April; effective that autumn. Joe Rains, elected on the same ballot, became the first president under the new name.
The August 1992 minutes appear under both titles — the organisation was 'still transitioning' at its first fall meeting.
The MyCampusToo committee was made a permanent standing committee and simultaneously renamed the Committee for Diversity and Inclusion, after some found the old name 'offensive and not inclusive.'

Among 13 constitutional amendments voted on 29 March 2024 were renamings of the executive posts; Director of Public Relations became Chief Communications Officer, announced open at the 24th Senate's first meeting.

Bill 21-25-S renamed the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Committee the Action and Opportunity Committee and retitled Chief Diversity Officers as Chief Engagement and Opportunity Officers, after Trump's executive order on DEI. Ratified by referendum with 88% in favour. Chair Megan Farmer said 'the committee at its core was not changing.'

patterns.name: The constitution as a permanent construction site
patterns.what_it_is: Constitutional revision is the single most repeated activity in the entire record. There is a revision committee, referendum, amendment package or full rewrite in more years than not, from the second year of the organisation's existence to the last year in the archive.
patterns.how_it_changed: Early revisions (1969-72) were fought section by section in public, with the Herald printing the proposed executive branch text and campaigning for a yes vote. From the 1980s they became routine internal housekeeping. The 2004 Convention was the only true structural rebuild. After 2004 the pattern became annual amendment packages, and by 2023-26 the work had turned largely custodial — fixing references to bodies that no longer existed.

instances.what: 27 February 1969: a committee appointed to study revision of the Associated Students constitution — the first revision effort, three years in.
4 November 1969: the proposed new constitution sent back for further study, with a limit on how long the review could run. 24 April 1970: four constitution changes go to a vote.
6 November 1970 the Congress was drafting a new constitution; 20 November it endorsed one; 26 January 1971 a committee opened a fresh study; 12 February 1971 that committee turned to judicial reform.

The Congress voted section by section (22 Feb 1972) with the Herald printing the full proposed executive-branch text; the executive branch was accepted 29 February; a 'Vote Yes' campaign ran ahead of a two-day referendum on 28-29 March. The archive does not show the referendum's result or turnout.
21 March 1975: the primary election was cancelled and a constitutional change approved in the same week.

Bill 2 (7 Sept 1976) created a constitutional revision committee in the congress's first month; revision stayed on the agenda all year and was the first of the four items Vogt recommended to the administration when she closed the congress on 26 April 1977.
8 September 1977: ASG reported still awaiting approval of changes to its constitution — the administration, not the students, held the final word.
30 November 1978: the congress approved a revised constitution.
17 March 1983 changes approved; Dean Charles Keown publicly questioned the revisions the following week; students voted on them on the same 14 April ballot that elected Jack Smith.

4 August 1986: 'the constitution of the WKU Associated Students with amendments' — twenty years of amendments consolidated into one document, and the only surviving snapshot of how the 1966 framework had been patched over two decades.

10 November 1987: constitutional amendments went before the body — 'the third straight year of structural revision attempts.' On 9 April 1987 an amendment had been defeated simply because too few members turned up to vote on it.
