TopSCHOLAR holds a constitution 'amended Spring 2002'; a 'Supremacy Clause' amendment passed in the April 2002 general election. The specific amendments are not detailed in the record.

The Constitutional Convention rebuilt the body into three branches — Executive Cabinet, Senate and Judicial Council. 'The most consequential clause is the quietest: every enrolled student became a member of SGA with the right to vote in its elections.' A Herald editorial on 16 March 2004 noted only 132 of about 18,000 students voted on it.
17 March 2005: students passed a package of 40 constitutional amendments, 1,193 to 262.

26 February / 1 March 2013: after two to three years of executive discussion the senate went through the constitution article by article, replacing class-year senate seats with college-based representation and guaranteeing seats for regional campuses.

The constitution as amended spring 2017 fixed the Senate at 36 seats: 3 each for senior, junior, sophomore and freshman classes, 2 graduate, 1 ESL international, 1 Gatton Academy, 6 academic-college and 14 at-large.

The Herald counted more than 15 proposed constitutional amendments in one year against about 10 the year before — the amendment rate itself became a symptom of the year Dahmer called 'almost toxic in nature.'

28 November 2023: three Legislative Operations bills corrected the governing documents — fixing references to a 'University Senate' that had split into separate Faculty and Staff senates, reconciling bylaws language about expelling senators with a constitution that only provides for impeachment, and updating drifted committee names.
24 February 2026: the 25th Senate adopted an official codified version of the Executive and Legislative Bylaws that 'shall supersede all prior versions.'

patterns.name: The student regent seat: created by statute, taken away and given back by statute, never by SGA
patterns.what_it_is: The single largest expansion of student power in the record was written in Frankfort, not in the SGA constitution. The seat was created by state legislation, carried no vote for years, was separately elected for most of its first two decades, merged into the presidency, and has split again three times when a president resigned.
patterns.how_it_changed: 1968: seat created, non-voting, filled by the Congress. 1970-72: campaigns for a vote fail repeatedly. 1982: a state bill changes how the regent is chosen, producing WKU's first campus-wide regent election. 1983: the president publicly insists the two offices are separate. By 1991 the same person holds both 'as was standard for this period.' The 2004 constitution had to keep a separate special election for the seat because state law governs it — which is exactly why the offices split again in 2006, 2009 and at every summer handover.

instances.what: 2 November 1967: 'Ward Favors Student on Board of Regents.' 8 December 1967: the Kentucky Intercollegiate Press Association backs student representation. 8 February 1968: a bill reaches committee; WKU sent lobbyists to Frankfort that month.
4 April 1968: William Menser 'assumes duties as Regent Board Member' — WKU's first student regent. 'The seat carried no vote at first.'

Kentucky's 1968 law required a student regent at every state campus. Because ASG president Bill Straeffer was an out-of-state student, the Congress of Associated Students elected Paul Gerard, a Bowling Green junior and junior class president, to the seat instead. He sat as a non-voting member on a two-year 1968-70 plate.

10 February 1970: students and faculty 'associate' regents press for a vote; an editorial calls for support of Senate Bill 75. 13 March 1970: the legislature drops the bill, under a headline that lawmakers had kept students impotent.

1 February 1972: 'Student Regent May Get Vote.' Four years after the seat was created it was still non-voting. Representation was arriving faster elsewhere: the Regents had seated eight students on the Academic Council in August 1970, and students won six votes on a university council in April 1972.

19 June 1974: Gregory McKinney sworn in as WKU's first African American student regent — seven years before Julius Price became the first Black gubernatorial appointee to the board. The student seat integrated the Board of Regents first.
Steve Henry held the student regent seat and the ASG presidency at the same time; the Herald's 30 April 1976 wrap-up described him 'balancing the twin jobs.'

28 January 1982: 'the regents bill, changing how the student regent was chosen, had passed the state House.' Five students then sought the seat in the first campus-wide election for it; no majority on 9 February forced a runoff, won by Sandra Norfleet on 16 February. Her term ran only from mid-February to roughly mid-April — a two-month stopgap.
3 February 1983: President Margaret Ragan published a Herald piece explaining that the ASG presidency and the student regent seat 'were now separate positions.'

22 May 1991: WKU's own On Campus newsletter reported Heather Falmlen as both Student Regent and ASG President — 'the two offices, separately elected two decades earlier, held by the same person.' In October 1991 Resolution 91-6-F asked student regent Falmlen to vote against re-electing Joe Iracane as board chair, evidence the seat by then carried a vote. The board re-elected him anyway a week later.

28 January 1992: Bill #92-01-S proposed a Student Advisory Committee — class presidents, a representative from each college, executive council ex officio — to brief the student regent on Board agenda items and canvass student opinion before each meeting.
'Because state law governs the student regent seat, the new constitution required a separate special election to fill it' — the one thing the Constitutional Convention could not absorb.

Watkins resigned as president and student regent on 28 November 2006, leaving students without a voting voice on the Board of Regents for at least a month. Jeanne Johnson won the February 2007 special election for the seat with 688 votes, 41 percent of ballots cast.

Boles resigned 30 January 2009. Kayla Shelton succeeded him as president but not as regent; the seat sat empty 26 days. The Judicial Council voted 2-1 to hold a special election over the Chief Justice's dissent and a written objection from the executive vice president. Reagan Gilley won 477-224 of 701 votes. For the rest of that year the two offices were held by two people.

The regent term outlasted the presidency: a Board resolution records Johnson serving 27 April 2007 to 18 July 2008, with Boles taking the oath the same day — months after he had been installed as SGA president.
Robinson was sworn in as regent 8 August 2025 and cast the lone vote against a $204, 1.69 percent tuition increase at his last board meeting on 5 June 2026, before handing the seat to Lucas.

patterns.name: Branches and committees: created, abolished, merged, and mostly reversible
patterns.what_it_is: The organisation has created and killed internal bodies continuously. A striking number are abolished and then reconstituted under a new name within months, or created by executive action rather than by the senate.
patterns.how_it_changed: The judicial function existed from the beginning but was only named a co-equal branch in 2004. Finance and diversity committees show the clearest abolish-and-rename cycle. From 2012 onward presidents increasingly created committees by executive action, and from 2016 the senate started converting ad hoc committees into permanent constitutional ones by referendum.

instances.what: 22 February 1968: Bill Martin's column questioned the Judicial Council's work; a letter the same month was headed 'Wanted: Work for Judicial Council.' The judicial body existed but had nothing to do.
5 December 1968: the Judicial Council began hearing student cases — 'an early exercise of the judicial power the young government claimed under its constitution.'
Bill 8 (8 March 1977) created a Complaint Committee to handle student grievances, in the same meeting the congress opposed a tuition increase.
15 February 1979: ASG established a Minorities Board, following the fall's push to add minority voices to the presidential screening process.

24 September 1985: the congress voted to abolish its own Finance Committee. On 2 April 1986 it wrote a Financial Advisory Council into the bylaws in its place — 'a structural change later reversed in part.'
25 March 1986: major/minor college representative seats created (Bill 86-19-S). 1 April 1986: revised SGA membership application process (Bill 86-21-S).
17 September 1996: the SGA Technology Committee created, to take up student email accounts.
Bill 99-10-F created the SGA position of Information Technology Director; a companion bill amended the constitution to include website guidelines.

24 September 2002, five days after members petitioned over missing gazebo funds: congress created an ad hoc Financial Review Committee and passed Bill 02-02-F creating a student position to serve as SGA's archivist.

The Convention formalised Executive Cabinet, Senate and Judicial Council, and created a Speaker of the Senate. The first speaker election, 15 April 2004, was won 9-8 and immediately questioned because the new constitution was unclear whether two-thirds of eligible voters or of total membership was required.
12 September 2012: SGA established a special long-term goals committee 'by executive action,' with at least eight members including students from outside SGA appointed by the president.
30 October 2014: a Cultural and Diversity Affairs Committee created; President Taylor said 'establishing ad hoc committees was a power she held as president.'

10 September 2015: an executive proposal created a Sustainability committee and Bill 2-15-F supported MyCampusToo. 12 October 2016: the SAVES committee (Standing Against Violence and Ending Self-harm) created.

16 November 2016: bills made Sustainability and MyCampusToo permanent standing committees under the constitution; students ratified that, plus SAVES, by referendum in April 2017. 15 February 2017: non-voting regional ambassador positions created for each regional campus, plus a South Campus liaison senator.

13 April 2023: Bill 44-23-S, a constitutional amendment merging the Community Relations and Outreach committees from 2023-24, which Speaker Mishchuk said 'would create a stronger committee amid low membership.'

29 November 2023: Bill 13-23-F raised the chief justice's required office hours from one to five per week and Bill 16-23-F required Judicial Council members to keep two office hours monthly — the judicial branch legislating its own workload.

The regional-campus bodies were built, defunded and rebuilt: student government went to Glasgow in October 1989 and helped rewrite its constitution; ASG cut Glasgow's budget in September 1990; SGA travelled to Glasgow in November 2012 to restart a dormant body, which ratified its own constitution on the same bylaws that month; in October 2014 Glasgow rewrote that constitution 'drastically' after struggling to retain members.

patterns.name: Senate size and who counts as a constituency
patterns.what_it_is: The chamber has been called Congress and Senate, has ranged from a handful of at-large congressmen to 50 members, and has repeatedly redefined which students get a guaranteed seat.
patterns.how_it_changed: From four executives plus two congressmen-at-large in 1968, through residence-hall and college representation in the late 1970s and 80s, to a 2013 rebuild that replaced class-year seats with college seats and guaranteed regional campuses, to a 36-seat constitutional formula in 2017 and a proliferation of identity- and status-based seats (international, Gatton, graduate, first-generation, transfer/non-traditional, ISEC, Honors) by 2024.

instances.what: The elected slate was President, Vice President, Secretary, Treasurer and two Congressmen at large. Total turnout 2,894, about 34 percent of the roughly 8,500 enrolment.

13 September 1979: ASG considered expanding residence hall representation in its congress; on 20 September a seats bill 'passed after being revised under pressure,' which the Herald called 'a small step in the right direction.'
1 March 1983: twenty-four students elected to the Associated Student Government Senate — the only hard seat count the archive preserves for the entire 1980s.
Only two of 32 congress positions were contested in the spring 1988 election.
29 March 1990: the congress voted to expand itself so that 'classes and student groups would get more voice.'

The senate opened 5 September 2006 with 18 seats and 8 senators present, swore in eight more that night, and had grown to 31 seats by 28 November. Quorum failed at the 5 December meeting with 16 of 31 present.

The Herald reported 50 total SGA members, of whom 21 — more than 40 percent — belonged to Greek organisations against less than 8 percent Greek membership campus-wide. Operating budget that year was $121,335, drawn from tuition.
36 senate seats. In the April 2011 election all 35 senate candidates were elected to the 36 open seats, 'each needing just one vote to win.'

A referendum on 19 September 2013 created a Navitas/ESL international student senate seat, passing with 310 of 426 votes (73 percent) — after the Judicial Council struck down an earlier version for violating WKU's non-discrimination clause and it was reworded in a six-minute emergency meeting. Boka said it would make WKU's the first student government in the state with an international senate seat.

36 seats fixed by constitution. On 28 February 2018 a bill replacing at-large and graduate seats with first-generation, transfer, non-traditional and ISEC senators failed 14-18. On 11 April 2018 the senate unanimously renamed the ESL international senator seat to international student senator.
3 April 2019: a senate seat for first-generation college students created 33-0. On 30 January 2019 nine senators had been forced to step down at once, leaving the chamber depleted.

19 September 2019: 'All 13 senators approved the yearly budget' — the working chamber had shrunk that far. By 5 February 2020 the SAVES and Sustainability chairs were both vacant with no replacements identified.

29 November 2023: Bill 14-23-F created a Mahurin Honors College senator seat, sponsored by the Judicial Council. Caden Lucas became its first occupant in September 2024 — and student body president in 2026.

22 March 2023: Bill 39-23-S, which would have moved the transfer, non-traditional and first-generation seats to the fall election and required a two-thirds vote before a vacant seat could be converted to an at-large seat, failed 19-15. Sponsor Neel Patel called the growing reliance on presidential appointments 'a dangerous practice for a government organization.'

34 senators elected from a field of over 60 candidates, five more seated in a fall special election. Three senators were removed 7-0 on 6 November 2024 under the provision requiring removal after a second censure.
The April 2025 ballot filled 13 at-large seats plus class, transfer/non-traditional, first-generation and college-specific seats — 'constituencies the 1966 constitution had no concept of.'

patterns.name: How officers were chosen: from a 34-percent turnout to unopposed tickets
patterns.what_it_is: Selection method has cycled through primaries and runoffs, campus-wide regent elections, judicial appeals, online balloting on TopNet, and repeated re-engineering of the election code — while the underlying problem, contest and turnout, never resolved.
patterns.how_it_changed: Direct spring election from the start, with primaries and runoffs by the mid-1970s; a separate fall senate election emerging by 1991; online TopNet voting from around 2004; Zoom and Instagram announcement by 2020-23. The rules governing candidacy — spending caps, GPA floors, prior-service requirements — were tightened and loosened repeatedly, each time framed as reform.

instances.what: Three candidates for the first presidency; the Herald warned of a 'popularity bandwagon' a week before campaigning opened, and closed the year with 'Goof Government Needs Student Vote.'
22 February 1974: ASG voted to retain its campaign spending limit rather than loosen the cap.

9 March 1978: spending limits set for the coming election. 11-18 April: losing candidate Ed Johnson contested the result and the Judicial Council denied his appeal after a long debate; the Herald had criticised the appeal system's lack of objectivity while the case was pending.
24 September 1981: ASG voted to increase its own campaign spending limit. The following April the general election results were voided outright and a repeat general election held on 20 April 1982.
31 October 1985: the congress debated setting a grade-point average requirement for its own members.

15 September 1988: ASG approved a ban on future write-in campaigns, five months after write-in votes threw its own presidential election into dispute. An editorial said the block showed ASG was not listening.

April 1999: Coates's initial 616-611 win narrowed to 614-611 on a recount; the finance vice-presidential race went 700-688 after a judicial review of campaign fliers; the Judicial Council overturned the spring election on 20 April. The Herald described a 'swath of scandal.' The pre-election issue also reported a debate over eliminating the rule requiring a year of SGA experience to run for office.

17 February and 2 March 2000: SGA rewrote its election codes 'to close loopholes,' ensure fairness between candidates and set campaign spending limits, ahead of the election Cassie Martin won 654-541.
18 March 2004: a two-day online election with 1,232 voters. Bradley said he was disappointed by the turnout.

Johnson defended the one-week campaign window written into election codes 'she said were inherited from past administrations,' warning that 'too much PR hurts,' as candidates blamed the codes for low turnout — 1,424 the year before, 1,376 the year before that.

Spending caps: $350 for president, $300 executive vice president, $250 administrative vice president, $50 senators. Taylor noted she ran unopposed and spent nothing, while Cain Alvey had spent every dollar of his $350 limit in the contested 2013 race.

23 March 2016: the senate refused to vote on election codes drafted by the Judicial Council that would have cut senate spending from $50 to $25 and limited candidates to three pieces of material per building. Richey called it 'too much red tape.'

15 February 2017: revised codes raised campaign spending allowances again, presidential candidates to $300. On 5 April a bill lowering SGA's GPA requirement from 2.5 to 2.0 passed 24-7 — 'receiving exactly the 24 votes needed from the 36-member senate' — after failing twice, and was ratified by referendum.

10 April 2017: the Judicial Council granted constitutional exemptions under Article 2.2.5 to two candidates who had served less than one semester, turning the presidential race into a three-way contest. 'Only Dahmer had been eligible under the constitution as written.'

19 September 2019: the senate halved campaign spending maximums — from $300 for president, $125 for the vice presidencies and $50 for senators — over the executive vice president's objection that turnout was 'awful.' Senator Symone Whalin argued poorer students were less likely to run for executive office.

29 March 2024: senators voted on 13 constitutional amendments including raising the senate and cabinet GPA floors back to 2.5 and 2.75 — undoing the 2017 reform — and allowing removal from office after two censures in one year.

Four consecutive presidential tickets ran effectively unopposed: Kurtz in 2023 and again in 2024 ('the ticket again ran unopposed on a ballot of more than 60 legislative candidates'), and Robinson in 2025 on a turnout of 966.

15 April 2026: a genuinely contested race between Lucas and Marshall drew 1,601 voters, 635 more than the year before — 'the clearest evidence in the whole record that WKU turnout tracks whether there is an actual contest.'

patterns.name: Structural changes that genuinely changed what SGA could do
patterns.what_it_is: A short list. Each of these altered the organisation's actual reach, and almost every one originated outside SGA's own constitution.

instances.what: The founding constitution plus Dean Charles Keown's 30 May 1967 memo to President Thompson proposing a student fee structure to create a budget for the Associated Student Government. Money made the body operational; the fee structure was proposed by the Dean of Students, not by students.

The 1968 state statute creating the student regent seat. It gave students a permanent chair in the room where tuition and fees are set — the only such power in the record — and SGA neither wrote nor could amend it.
The 1982 state regents bill changing how the student regent was chosen, producing the first campus-wide election for the seat. State law, again, restructured SGA.

The Constitutional Convention: three branches drawn from the student body at large, and every enrolled student made a member of SGA with the right to vote in its elections. It converted a club with a congress into a body claiming the whole student body as its constituency.

The first student referendum in SGA history — the $3 Revolution 91.7 radio fee, passed 1,066-765 in April 2003 and sent to the Board of Regents. It established that SGA could put a binding fee question to students, a mechanism used again for the $9 Talisman fee in 2005 and the football referendum in 2006.

The DUC renovation: SGA had to pass resolutions on the design and fees before the Board of Regents could approve the project. The senate tabled the bill in December 2010 for lack of student input, delaying the Board presentation from January to April, then passed a resolution on 22 February 2011 capping cost at $49,128,545 with a fee of up to $70 a semester for 20 years. A veto point that actually bit.

The Pass/D/Fail campaign: after Associate Provost Rob Hale rebuffed SGA, a petition drew more than 3,500 signatures in three days, the Faculty Senate voted 40-9 and SGA unanimously, and on 1 December 2020 the provost reversed the university's position. Power exercised through mobilisation, not through any clause.

1 October 2025: WKU General Counsel told the Senate that House Bill 4 binds SGA's spending because SGA receives university money, that it could fund organisations and events only if content neutral, and that the statute counts social media and digital content as a resource. The Pride Center lost its university-related status. A genuine reduction in SGA's discretion, imposed entirely from outside.

patterns.name: Reform that was cosmetic
patterns.what_it_is: Changes framed as structural reform that left the organisation's capacity untouched — renamings, symbolic committees, procedural tinkering, and self-evaluations with no follow-through in the record.

instances.what: Bill 6 (15 February 1977) proposed that ASG 'conduct a self-evaluation for the purposes of transparency and improvement.' The archive holds the bill and nothing about a result. In the same session the congress rejected a resolution on discrimination with fourteen members abstaining.

The proposed title change and the new-logo resolution both went nowhere; the congress voted to keep the present logo. Meanwhile the year's real fight was over dormitory room inspections, which ASG voted down, then re-endorsed after nearly sleeping through its own vote.
Abolishing the Finance Committee in September 1985 and writing a Financial Advisory Council into the bylaws in April 1986 — the same function under a new name, seven months apart.

18 September 1986: 'a minor change in voting' procedures, described as the first structural tinkering of the Todd presidency. On 5 March 1987 the congress suspended its rules to pass a batch of bills in one meeting, and on 9 April a constitutional amendment failed because too few members turned up.

13 February 2014: an amendment stripping the president's sole power to appoint Judicial Council justices and raising the council to seven justices passed at the Tuesday meeting — then the Executive Council reviewed the constitution and determined too few senators had attended for the vote to count, sending it back to first read. The reform was undone by the same attendance problem it was meant to address.

Moving committee-chair appointments from the president to the speaker of the senate failed twice — on 5 April 2017 and again 26-2 on 28 March 2018, with Speaker Ryan Richardson saying 'I 100 percent do not support this bill.' The appointment power never moved.

Bill 5-17-F, barring the executive branch from writing legislation, failed 4-8 at the first meeting of the year. In a year of more than 15 proposed amendments and an emergency Judicial Council meeting, the outgoing executive vice president called the year 'awful' and 'an absolute hell.'

The 20 April 2020 'emergency clause' amendment allowing cabinet terms to be extended until the following election under judicial oversight — necessary housekeeping, but the only constitutional response the archive records to a year in which the campus closed.
6 October 2021: Bill 2.21f barred the speaker of the senate from voting on legislation 'to avoid bias,' passing 21-2, alongside two bills scrubbing obsolete 2007-era bylaws.

Bill 21-25-S renaming the DEI Committee the Action and Opportunity Committee. The senate initially lacked the 21 members needed for a two-thirds vote and phoned absent members onto Zoom to reach quorum. Co-author Gammons 'called the change mostly a formality'; chair Farmer said the committee 'at its core was not changing.' Ratified by 88 percent of voters.

patterns.name: Powers gained, powers lost, powers shed
patterns.what_it_is: Beyond the regent seat, the organisation's practical authority has moved through three areas: the budget, campus entertainment and services, and academic policy. It shed one of these outright.
patterns.how_it_changed: ASG ran concerts and lost money on them through the 1970s until the function became untenable and was dropped. Budget control has been steadily formalised but the total is set by the university and has been flat or falling since 2013. Academic-policy intervention is the one area where the organisation has repeatedly won.

instances.what: The entertainment role collapsed: a September 1975 concert drew 4,300 and lost $7,000; in February 1975 the Herald reported financial difficulties might force ASG to drop its entertainment duties; the Seals and Crofts show lost $3,800 in November 1976; by April 1975 the outgoing congress was abandoning plans for a final concert. ASG never recovered the function.

25 January 1979: 'The Associated Student Government faced losing control over student activities funding — a direct threat to one of the government's core powers.' The archive does not show how the fight was resolved.

Bill #91-6-S changed the by-laws on overriding a presidential veto; the new procedure was tested weeks later when the emergency-kit resolution survived a veto on 14 March 1991 — 'the only veto fight reported in the Herald index that year.'

The faculty-evaluation campaign: Resolution 00-2-S (April 2000) asked the Faculty Senate to approve a mandatory published evaluation from fall 2000; by November 2004 SGA had scaled back to a five-question pilot posted on TopNet; the plus/minus grading fight ran from 2003 until Provost Barbara Burch declined to implement it on 24 April 2007, with President Johnson saying SGA 'had raised awareness and led student protests.'

Two clean academic wins: Provost Emslie dropped the bi-term and per-credit-hour tuition proposal on 21 February 2013 after SGA and the University Senate both passed resolutions against it, and the Board of Regents committee unanimously approved SGA's teaching assistant evaluation policy on 29 March 2013.

3 December 2013: the Judicial Council ruled a senate motion reversing SGA's Talisman fee stance unconstitutional — and ruled the original 2005 policy unconstitutional too, because it 'was never passed according to SGA policy.' The judiciary invalidating a decade-old student referendum position.

3 December 2015: the Judicial Council voided $1,500 for the physics department and up to $759 for the art department under Bylaw 6.1, which states SGA may allocate funds solely to students. An internal rule narrowing the body's own spending reach.

Budget trajectory: $105,000 (2003-04), $110,000 (2004-05), $115,000 with $24,000 left unspent (2005-06), $121,335 (2010-11), $125,000 or $6.25 per student (2013-14), $138,500 then cut $19,500 (2015-16, against the University of Louisville's $1.2 million), $100,000 after a $15,000 cut (2018-19), and $100,000 flat through 2024-25 and 2025-26. On 10 May 2013 university budget cuts removed the automatic Higher Education Price Index increase SGA had received.

26 January 2016: SGA refused to supply the enforcement corps for the campus smoking phaseout. 'SGA has no intention on actually being the group that enforces this,' Richey said. A power declined rather than lost.

21 April 2017: President Ransdell stated within days that Resolution 6-17-S, the reparations resolution passed 19-10-1, 'was not a university position.' National wire coverage followed. Both authors described it as a conversation starter — the clearest case in the record of SGA's legislative reach ending at the resolution itself.

7 November 2019: Chief Justice Isaac Keller told senators the Alpha Xi Delta resolution 'would be purely symbolic because SGA cannot direct WKU to defund an organization on grounds of discrimination.' The executive board had already vetoed it 4-0 and the senate sustained the veto.

patterns.name: Self-evaluation as a recurring ritual
patterns.what_it_is: From the first year onward, SGA and the Herald have produced a near-annual verdict on whether the organisation works. The verdict is remarkably stable across sixty years, and it rarely produces a structural change.

instances.what: 27 October 1966: the Herald judged leaders were performing well but failing to communicate with the students they represented — 'the first public report card on the year-old government.' The May 1967 year-end review summed the first year as 'organization, progress and apathy.'
29 April 1968: 'Past Performance of Associated Student Government Analyzed' ran as Menser's term ended. 'The archive does not yet hold the text of either article, only their headlines.'

16 April 1974: Al Cross's retrospective, 'Presidency Ends for Steve Yater; One Major Program Started' — 'the archive does not yet hold the article's text, only its headline crediting his administration with a single major accomplishment.'
15 October 1974: 'Protesters urged a revamping of the Associated Student Government,' in the same issue reporting ASG ecology projects were non-existent.

27 April 1976: a special Herald supplement 'paid for and written by the Associated Student Government' summing up the year's wins, and printing the year's roster of congress members and its bills and resolutions — SGA self-evaluating in public, at its own expense.
Bill 6, 15 February 1977: ASG to conduct a self-evaluation 'for the purposes of transparency and improvement.'
29 October 1987: the Herald ran an article arguing 'apathy was killing both Associated Student Government and the Residence Hall Association.'
12 December 1988: 'members rated their own organization as average,' in the same issue that reported ASG dropping its push for a weeklong Thanksgiving break three weeks after voting to seek one.

10 December 1998: Vice President Matthew Bastin circulated a memo of the fall's passed legislation to the advisor, officers, committee heads and the Herald's editor, answering accusations of unproductiveness. 'The list itself was the rebuttal.'
29 November 2001: dueling opinion pieces — President Leslie Bedo's 'Meeting Goals of Student Government Association, But Not Students'' and Troy Ransdell's reply, 'Action, Not Complaints.'
12 September 2012: a special long-term goals committee established so it 'could draw up a set of goals to focus on for the next few years.'

27 May 2015: Richey used social media to be 'very transparent with the WKU Student Government Association budget' — while noting SGA had not yet received its budget and he had not been told how much remained from the prior year.
19 April 2017: students ratified a referendum requiring more accessible executive discretionary spending reports.

28 November 2023: three bills correcting the organisation's own governing documents, including reconciling bylaws that provided for expelling senators with a constitution that only provides for impeachment.

14 April 2026: Legislative Operations Chair Caden Lucas reported the 25th Senate had passed 56 pieces of legislation, 'the most since the 2018-2019 school year' — the organisation measuring itself by volume.

Donald Smith, president 1993-94 and later president of the College Heights Foundation, told the Herald in 2022 that 'while the structure had changed over the years, the fundamental principle for SGA to be a voice for the students has remained unphased.'

patterns.name: Where the archive goes quiet, and what that hides
patterns.what_it_is: The record is not evenly thick. It is dense on legislation and named officers for 1966-1978 and again from 2004 onward, and structurally thin for roughly 1979-2003. Any claim about how the organisation was shaped in those years rests on far less evidence than the rest.
patterns.how_it_changed: Sourcing shifts from digitised Herald indexes (headlines only, often without article text) in the early decades, to SGA's own numbered legislation and minutes from the 1990s, to full minutes and constitutions posted on the web from about 2006.

instances.what: Reed Morgan sits on a single-year 1968 plate as 'unresolved.' Re-checked 4 August 2026: fresh searches 'turned up only the same 1963-67 WKU Forensics team roster and the 1966 constitution-committee material already cited. Nothing new for 1968-69. No source describes him as president.'

The plaque's 1970-71 pairing of Lyne and Zielke 'conflates two separate one-year terms' — Zielke's term was 1969-70. Plaque error, not archive gap, but it means the succession itself had to be reconstructed from election coverage.

The constitutional referendum of 28-29 March 1972 is the most consequential structural vote of the decade and 'the archive does not yet show the referendum's result or turnout.' The KCLU court action connected to Associated Students and Linda Jones's published correction of the Herald both survive as headlines only.

'The archive does not yet show what Hargrove's administration passed or fought over during 1979-80 beyond the record's general sweep of the year. Further Herald issues from the fall and spring semester have not yet been checked.' A full presidential year is effectively blank on structure.

Todd sits on a two-year 1986-88 plate. On election day 1987 'the Herald endorsed challenger Greg Elder and headlined the race itself as no contest. The indexed issues that survive do not record the published result.' Whether the 1987-88 president was elected is not established.

Only one senate seat count survives for the entire decade — the 24 senators elected on 1 March 1983. Committee structure for the 1980s is known only from the 1985-86 Finance Committee/Financial Advisory Council pair and the 1986-87 Judicial Council roster filed with the amended constitution.

Repeated across years: 'Archive does not preserve a full senate officer list or seat count for this year' (1990-91, 1991-92, 1995-96, 1996-97). For 1992-93, minutes from 25 Aug 1992 to 13 Apr 1993 survive but 'no full officer list, committee structure, or seat count survives beyond the president.' For 1997-98 at least 24 numbered bills survive from one semester but no officer list beyond president and secretary.

'TopSCHOLAR's full-text PDFs for this year sit behind an automated-access check and have not been read. The ad hoc financial review committee formed in the gazebo-funds dispute is the only committee identified by name in confirmed sources.'

The exception that proves the rule: Resolutions 93-4-F through 93-20-F survive in the correspondence files — 'the fullest single-semester record in the collection, and the best available answer to how much a WKU student senate actually passes in a working term.'

Even in the digital era the record contradicts itself on structure: the Herald called Isaac Keller executive vice president, ran a correction changing it to administrative vice president, and had already given that same title to Abbey Norvell in September. 'Sourcing does not resolve which title is correct.'

notes:
Evidence is entirely from /Users/samkurtz/Downloads/sga60/data/years.json, read in full (61 year records, all events, leader profiles, notes, organization blocks and document entries). No external sources consulted and no files edited. A flattened working copy was written to the session scratchpad only (/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-samkurtz/d305ae30-4294-46a3-abb0-409743beff17/scratchpad/flat.txt); the source file was not modified.

Two things worth flagging about method. First, the archive's own metadata says the plaque is person-keyed and several people report their year on it is wrong; several structural claims (Zielke/Lyne 1969-71, Reed Morgan 1968, the two 1914-15 Seay/Taylor plates) are the file's corrections of the plaque rather than independent evidence, and I have used them as the file presents them. Second, the file is markedly denser on legislation than on structure. Claims about senate size, committee rosters and constitutional text before roughly 2004 rest on a handful of surviving artefacts — chiefly the 4 August 1986 consolidated constitution, the 1 March 1983 senate election, and scattered bill numbers — while the post-2004 record includes posted constitutions, bylaws and minutes. Where a decade is thin I have said so rather than inferring continuity.

One structural question the archive raises but does not answer: the file records ASG "awaiting approval of changes to its constitution" in September 1977 and Dean Charles Keown publicly questioning the 1983 revisions, but never states whether university approval of constitutional amendments was a standing requirement after 1966. That is a real limit on any claim about how much the organisation could change itself.

seam: The archive shows an organisation whose real, enforceable power points inward and whose external power is almost entirely evidentiary. Inside its own walls SGA can do anything: void an election (1982), overturn one (1999), disqualify a president-elect (2013), disqualify a whole ticket mid-vote (2018), censure a sitting vice president 6-0 (2024), remove three senators 7-0 (2024), veto a unanimously passed resolution (2017), rewrite its constitution in 1969, 1972, 1975, 1976, 1978, 1983, 1987, 1993, 2002, 2004, 2005, 2013, 2017, 2024, 2025 and codify a full bylaw rewrite in 2026. Outside its walls it has never once compelled anything. The Board of Regents re-elected Joe Iracane a week after SGA asked it not to (1991); it approved the Confucius Institute and declined to revisit the contract - "it's a done deal" (2015); it raised the athletics fee 8-2 over the student regent's dissent (2000), the construction fee 9-1 over her abstention (2006), tuition 9 percent after her 6-percent cap motion died with two votes (2008), and tuition $204 over the student regent's lone no vote (2026). Administrators renamed Downing Student Union after the senate voted 19-8 against it (2013), renamed the student-chosen pub (2016), left SGA's housing-diversity resolution out of the ten-year plan (2017), and rejected the reparations resolution within days (2017). The single sharpest artefact of the ceiling is 2013: SGA's Judicial Council disqualified president-elect Keyana Boka 3-2, she appealed to Vice President for Student Affairs Howard Bailey, he reinstated her, and the council concluded in an emergency meeting that it did not believe it had the power to contest him - Chief Justice Seth Church calling it "a serious infringement on our autonomy." The student judiciary discovered it was not final. What SGA actually wins outside itself, it wins by producing evidence somebody else can act on: 1,500 signatures against plus/minus grading (2003, dropped by the provost in 2007), a 1,066-765 referendum that sent the radio fee to the Regents (2003), 3,500 P/D/F petition signatures in three days plus twenty pages of testimony (2020, granted). It is a body with a fully articulated internal state and a purely advisory external one, and the sixty-year record is the sound of it discovering that over and over.

patterns.name: Disputed elections and the judiciary that adjudicates them
patterns.what_it_is: The single most reliable conflict in the record. A losing candidate, an anonymous complaint or a rules technicality throws the result into the hands of the Judicial Council, which then decides who governs. It happens in every decade from the 1970s on.
patterns.span: 1978 to 2022, at least fifteen documented episodes
patterns.how_it_changed: It began as an appeal by a losing candidate heard by a body the Herald said lacked objectivity (1978), became a habit of voiding and re-running elections (1982, 1984, 1990, 1999), and matured after the 2004 Constitutional Convention into a formal judicial power to disqualify winners outright (2013, 2018). The 2013 Boka case established the ceiling: a Vice President for Student Affairs can reverse the student court, and the court concluded it could not contest him. After that the council still rules, but it rules knowing it can be overruled - by 2022 it was clearing candidates rather than removing them.

instances.what: Ed Johnson, having lost the presidency to Steve Thornton, contested the result; the Judicial Council denied his appeal on 18 April after a long debate. The Herald had criticised the appeal system's lack of objectivity while the case was pending.
The general election results were voided, a decision the Herald said disgusted the candidates. A repeat general election was held 20 April, which Margaret Ragan won.
LaMont Jones dropped out of an ASG revote; the disputed election requiring a revote marked the low point of the fall semester.

Scott Whitehouse won on 7 April amid editorials saying oversight and closed minds had marred the process; Bruce Cambron called for a new election a week later over write-in votes ASG was told it could not ignore. The congress banned write-in campaigns in September 1988, and Cambron took his complaint to university president Thomas Meredith in October - six months on.

Heather Falmlen won "amid Associated Student Government election protests," with a rival group urging a boycott of the vote, an editorial calling the contest's "immature antics" a disappointment, and a published complaint that the Herald's own coverage was biased.

On election day the Herald reported presidential candidate Scott Sivley had been warned by SGA for violating campaign policies; the April primary was reported as disputed for his not following SGA and university procedures.

The worst year on record. Amanda Coates's 616-611 win narrowed to 614-611 on a recount she requested; Joe Matheis beat Ryan Morrison 700-688 for finance VP only after the judicial council reviewed and let stand a campaign-flier violation, and Morrison then filed a complaint disputing that decision; a letter to the editor questioned SGA's investigation of fliers reading "Vote for Will Jones in Racism" that targeted the first Black presidential candidate in years. On 20 April the Judicial Council overturned the spring election outright, amid what one opinion piece called a "swath of scandal."

Robert Watkins was elected the first speaker of the senate 9-8 under the new constitution, with three members present barred from voting by a judicial council ruling and the constitution unclear whether two-thirds of eligible or total membership was required. Jessica Martin warned of a "semester of frustration"; the result stood.
After Johnathon Boles's Red Towel Party ticket won, Skylar Jordan filed a complaint against the party; the SGA council took no action on 22 April and the result stood.

The Judicial Council voted 3-2 in an emergency meeting to disqualify president-elect Keyana Boka over a self-promotional email sent to Honors College students, on a complaint by runner-up Cain Alvey, who stood to become president. Boka appealed to Vice President for Student Affairs Howard Bailey, who reinstated her; on 16 April the council unanimously decided it did not believe it had the power to challenge his memorandum, while recording official disapproval.

"Postergate": anonymous accusations alleged Jay Todd Richey had breached election codes on poster placement. The judicial council warned him against future violations and confirmed he had rightfully won.

In an emergency meeting two days before results, the Judicial Council disqualified the entire Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson presidential ticket and a senate candidate over a Pepe the Frog image in campaign chalkings, and suspended Kenan Mujkanovic's campaign separately. It then reversed the disqualification to a suspension; Mayer won with 35 percent of 2,378 votes. The campaign called it a "secret meeting."

The Judiciary Council held an hour-long Zoom hearing on complaints that candidate Cole Bornefeld's student-wide email about Swipe Out Hunger violated the code's self-promotion ban. Speaker Tess Welch argued the signature made it self-promotion; the council voted in favour of his campaign.

patterns.name: The election code itself as a permanent battleground
patterns.what_it_is: Separate from disputed results: the recurring fight over the rules of campaigning - spending caps, campaign length, who may run, which seats appear on which ballot. Every generation rewrites them and the next generation calls them outdated.
patterns.how_it_changed: The 1970s and 1980s fought over one number, the spending cap, raising and holding it. From 2000 the argument became explicitly about fairness and access: closing loopholes (2000), whether one-week campaigns suppress turnout (2008), whether high caps price out poorer candidates (2019), and by 2023 whether presidential appointment of vacant seats had displaced election altogether. The direction of travel reverses repeatedly - caps go up in 2017 and are halved in 2019 - which is itself the finding: no settled theory, just whichever faction holds the senate.

instances.what: ASG voted to retain its campaign spending limit rather than loosen the cap on campaign outlays.
The Associated Student Government set spending limits for candidates ahead of the spring election that would choose Moore's successor.
ASG voted to increase its campaign spending limit, after a week of debate over whether the cap should rise.

The Herald covered proposed new election codes intended to close loopholes, then reported they were meant to ensure fairness between candidates and set campaign spending limits - coverage running through the same weeks as the Martin-Wright race.

Candidates criticised the one-week campaign window as part of SGA's low-involvement problem. Red Towel candidate Tedde Harden promised to rework what he called outdated election codes; President Jeanne Johnson said her administration had inherited them and warned that "too much PR hurts."

Spending caps stood at $350 for president, $300 for executive VP, $250 for administrative VP and $50 for senators. Nicki Taylor said she ran unopposed and did not spend a cent, but noted Cain Alvey had spent every dollar of his $350 limit in the contested 2013 race.

The senate declined to even vote on election codes drafted by the Judicial Council that would have cut senate campaign spending from $50 to $25 and limited candidates to three pieces of material per building. Richey, absent, called it "too much red tape."
Senators approved revised codes raising campaign spending allowances, with presidential candidates permitted $300 - one year after refusing to lower them.

The senate halved the maximums again, over the objection of Executive Vice President Garrett Edmonds, who called SGA turnout "awful." Senator Symone Whalin argued poorer students were less likely to be able to run for executive office.

Bill 39-23-S, which would have moved the transfer, non-traditional and first-generation seats to the fall election and required a two-thirds vote to convert a vacant seat into an at-large seat, failed 19-15. Gatton Academy senator Neel Patel called the growing reliance on presidential appointments "a dangerous practice for a government organization."

patterns.name: Impeachment, censure and removal
patterns.what_it_is: The organisation's formal disciplinary machinery, used against senators, justices, vice presidents and - once - a sitting president.
patterns.span: 1976 to 2024, with a near-total documentary gap between 1976 and 2004
patterns.how_it_changed: The first documented case is an acquittal (Faulk, 1976). For nearly thirty years afterwards the archive records no impeachment at all - discipline appears only as absenteeism enforcement. It reappears in 2004 as articles of impeachment that die on a technicality, and from 2009 becomes routine and bureaucratic: absence removals with vote counts, censure hearings brought by the cabinet against its own vice president, and a 2024 constitutional amendment making two censures in one year automatic grounds for removal. The 2023 Bornefeld case marks the outer limit - the Speaker of the Senate took her own president to the Judicial Council over anti-transgender Instagram likes, lost unanimously, and a Title IX report seeking his removal was filed two days later; the constitutional route required 20 percent of the Senate, a fourteen-day wait and a two-thirds vote, and never ran.

instances.what: The Associated Student Government opened impeachment hearings against congress member Gerard Faulk on 26 March, the same week candidates including Christy Vogt were set to speak. He was acquitted on 9 April, the same issue that reported Vogt's election win. A Herald editorial held up ASG's troubles as a cautionary example for the university's newly forming Faculty Senate.
The Herald reported that former president Bob Moore had been found ineligible for an Associated Student Government job. The archive does not hold the article's account of why.
ASG moved to get tough on absenteeism after a member lost his seat the week before.

Senator Josh Collins drafted articles of impeachment against president-elect Nick Todd's outgoing finance vice presidency after the judicial council found $611 missing from the SGA Dining Dollars account. The council ruled a two-week impeachment process could not be completed before he left that office anyway. He was sworn in as president with the investigation unresolved, and resigned that July.

Chief Justice Stuart Kenderes reported the Judicial Council had removed Senator Theodore Harden for excessive unexcused absences; he did not attend the council meeting to defend himself. Senator Vashae Swope was reviewed and allowed to remain.

Ten of 36 senators were called before the judicial board for excessive absences; Kevin Adams and Kevin Preston were dismissed after failing to attend their hearings, which the council read as intent to resign. In February 2012 President Billy Stephens simply reappointed Adams, saying the two were good friends who had stayed close after the removal.

The Judicial Council voted unanimously not to censure Senator John Winstead over an "impeach Ransdell" sign and a Facebook image mocking the president, finding his conduct protected by the First Amendment. Winstead said the fact he was investigated at all was "the problem I'm objecting to." Chief Justice Kelsey Luttrell resigned effective the end of the semester, saying the council had been publicly ridiculed and lacked support from fellow members.

The Judicial Council censured Public Relations Chair Will Hurst at an emergency meeting after finding the executive board had complied with the constitution in advertising the fall election, against Hurst's complaint of a vote-total discrepancy between amendments that passed and failed.

An impeachment hearing for Associate Justice Annalicia Carlson was scheduled and then cancelled after SGA determined too few senators would attend. The petition accused her of inconsistently listing candidates by preferred or legal name and of overstepping during Wood Brown's failed confirmation. Carlson, graduating that week, called it a waste of resources showing "the pettiness of the organization."

Speaker of the Senate Yulia "Julie" Mishchuk requested a censure hearing against President Cole Bornefeld over anti-transgender posts he had liked on Instagram, with Queer Student Union members and both vice presidents attending. The Judicial Council voted unanimously against censure. Two days later a Title IX report was filed with Student Conduct seeking his removal.

The Judicial Council voted 6-0 to censure Administrative Vice President Salvador León after a hearing brought by the executive cabinet, over a $425.25 Preston Center deposit spent before Bill 22-23-S passed. León produced texts in which Kurtz replied "sweet" and "bet sounds good"; the council found the spending improper, recommended no further discipline and called it a learning experience. That November it removed three senators 7-0 under the provision requiring removal after a second censure.

patterns.name: Vetoes and override attempts
patterns.what_it_is: The executive branch striking down what the senate has passed, and the senate's usually-failed attempt to strike back. Structurally impossible before the three-branch constitution, but the fight predates it in cruder forms.
patterns.span: 1981 to 2019, concentrated after the 2004 Constitutional Convention
patterns.how_it_changed: Before 2004 the archive records vetoes only as isolated Herald index lines - a 1981 veto of a lobbyist plan, a 1991 by-law rewrite of the override procedure that was immediately tested, one unnamed vetoed resolution in 1996. After 2004 the veto becomes a live executive weapon used against the senate's most contested votes, and the override becomes the senate's most reliable failure: 2014 and 2019 both ended with the veto sustained. In 2017 the veto of a unanimously passed resolution cost SGA the author, who resigned the same night.

instances.what: The Associated Student Government vetoed a plan to pay an education lobbyist, weeks after rallying publicly for higher education funding.

Bill #91-6-S amended the by-laws on overriding a presidential veto. The new procedure was tested weeks later, on 14 March, when the senate's emergency-kit resolution survived a veto and stood as passed - the only veto fight in the Herald index that year.
The Herald reported SGA proposing more campus lighting while a resolution was vetoed.

After the Tuesday senate meeting the executive board vetoed a bill financing community and campus projects through civic engagement grants, its first veto of the year. The Herald reported the grants were "a reality for only about 30 minutes" and that time restraints halted an appeal.

Resolution 11-14-F supporting a smoke-free campus passed the senate 14-10 and was vetoed by the Executive Cabinet after the meeting. At the final meeting of the semester the override failed, and President Nicki Taylor read out the cabinet's statement citing enforcement, housing requirements and practicality.

Senator Chase Coffey's resolution letting former senators who resigned in good standing attend the end-of-year banquet passed the senate unanimously, then was vetoed by the Executive Council as unconstitutional. Coffey resigned the same night.

The executive board vetoed Resolution 4-19-F, seeking discipline against Alpha Xi Delta after a video showed members singing a racial slur, by 4-0 with two abstentions; the senate sustained it. President Will Harris, who abstained, said the discrimination claim would have to come from the Student Code of Conduct and no violation had been noted. Senators raised his standing as an Alpha Xi Delta knight; he rejected it as grounds for bias.

patterns.name: Rewriting the constitution
patterns.what_it_is: Structural self-revision, pursued in almost every decade, usually while the body is being told it is ineffective. The most persistent single activity in the record.
patterns.how_it_changed: The early rewrites (1969-72) were about building a government at all, and passed by referendum. From the mid-1970s to the 1980s revision became annual maintenance - the 1986 archive holds "twenty years of amendments consolidated into one document," the only surviving snapshot of how the 1966 framework had been patched. The 2004 Constitutional Convention was the break: three branches, and the quietest clause the most consequential - every enrolled student became a member of SGA with the right to vote in its elections. Only 132 of about 18,000 students voted on it. From 2013 the rewrites became representational engineering - college seats, regional campus seats, an international seat, a first-generation seat, a Mahurin Honors seat - and by 2025 defensive, renaming the DEI Committee under federal pressure.

instances.what: The Associated Student Government returned its proposed new constitution for further study while limiting how long the review could run; four constitution changes went to a vote in April 1970; the Congress endorsed a proposed constitution in November 1970 and a study committee reached judicial-reform provisions by February 1971.

Jones's Congress voted section by section on a rewritten constitution on 22 February with the executive branch's full text printed in the Herald, accepted the executive branch on 29 February, and put the document to a two-day referendum at the end of March under a "Vote Yes" campaign. The archive does not show the referendum's result or turnout.

Bill 2, passed 7 September 1976, created a constitutional revision committee within the congress's first month. Vogt closed her term on 26 April 1977 with constitutional revision first among four recommendations to the administration.

ASG approved changes to its constitution in March, and Dean Charles Keown publicly questioned the revisions the following week. Students voted on the revisions on the same April ballot that elected Jack Smith.

The constitution of the WKU Associated Students with amendments was compiled - the only surviving snapshot of how the 1966 framework had been patched over two decades, with a Judicial Council roster for 1986-87 alongside it.

Constitutional amendments went before the body in November; the archive notes it was the third straight year of structural revision attempts. In April an amendment died because too few members turned up to vote on it.

The Constitutional Convention created three branches - Executive Cabinet, Senate and Judicial Council - drawn from the student body at large, and made every enrolled student a member of SGA with the right to vote in its elections. A Herald editorial noted only 132 of about 18,000 students voted on it.

The senate passed most of a package of constitutional amendments after two to three years of executive discussion, replacing class-year senate seats with college-based representation and guaranteeing seats for regional campuses such as Glasgow and Owensboro. It stripped out the bylaw that would have made serving SGA members ineligible for SGA-sponsored scholarships.

Students ratified all six referendums, making the SAVES, MyCampusToo and Sustainability committees permanent, lowering the GPA requirement to 2.0, creating regional campus ambassadors and requiring more accessible executive discretionary spending reports.

Bill 21-25-S restructured the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Committee as the Action and Opportunity Committee following President Trump's executive order. The senate initially lacked the 21 members needed for two-thirds, phoned absent officers onto Zoom to reach quorum, then passed it unanimously; the student body ratified it with 88 percent.

patterns.name: Resignations and mid-term collapse of the executive
patterns.what_it_is: Presidents, vice presidents, chief justices and blocs of senators walking out mid-year, usually leaving a constitutional problem behind - most acutely, who holds the student seat on the Board of Regents.
patterns.how_it_changed: Early resignations were individual protests (Glass in 1973). From 1982 they began removing presidents, and after the president and student regent merged into one office the resignations started leaving WKU's governing board without a student in it: at least a month in 2006, twenty-six days in 2009. The 2009 case is the clearest illustration of the seam - because state law governs the regent seat, SGA could hand the presidency to its executive vice president but could not hand her the regency, and a 2-1 Judicial Council vote over the sitting EVP's written objection was needed to call a special election.

instances.what: ASG representative Reginald Glass resigned his post in protest, an early sign of strain inside the congress.

President Marcel Bush resigned on 14 January, reported the same week as the retrospective on his term. Board of Regents minutes of 30 January name David Payne, then vice president, as the new SGA president, filling the balance of the 1981-82 term.
Vice president William Chandler quit; within a week three people had been nominated for ASG positions.

Amos Gott and Van Hodge stepped down as ASG officers in the same week the remaining officers clashed publicly over comprehensive exams. Karl Miller was picked as public relations vice president two weeks later.

Nick Todd, elected president in March with 772 of 1,232 votes, resigned in July citing personal conflicts, after an April investigation into more than $600 misused from an SGA Dining Dollars account. Executive Vice President Katie Dawson acted as president over the summer; Patti Johnson was the only student to show interest and won a September special election with 1,291 votes.

Rob Watkins's resignation as president and student regent was read into the senate's minutes on 28 November, after senators aired concerns about him at an unannounced 10 p.m. meeting the night before. A Herald editorial that week was headlined "SGA actions an embarrassment to Western." Students were left without a voting voice on the Board of Regents for at least a month.

Johnathon Boles resigned on 30 January for health reasons. Kayla Shelton succeeded him as president but not as student regent. The Judicial Council voted 2-1 on 10 February to hold a special election, over Chief Justice Lisa Kappler's dissent and a written objection from Executive Vice President Skylar Jordan that it was unnecessary; Kappler resigned two days later. Reagan Gilley won on 25 February, 477 to 224, after 26 days with the seat empty.

Three senators - Michel Stephens, Emmett Stephens and Daniel Shaw - resigned at the 20 October meeting over President Kevin Smiley's nomination of Greg Capillo to the Student Publications Committee, which helps choose the Herald's editor-in-chief. Smiley called the accusations of favouritism and corruption unfounded.
Chief Justice Kelsey Luttrell resigned two days after her council declined to censure Senator Winstead, saying the council had been publicly ridiculed and lacked support from fellow SGA members.
SGA opened the spring semester with nine senators required to step down from their positions, leaving the chamber depleted; no new legislation was introduced at the meeting.

Speaker of the Senate Nathan Terrell resigned and quit the executive vice president race after a video showing him using a racial slur was sent anonymously to the Herald; he first denied being in it, then confirmed it and left the Edmonds ticket.

Chief Justice Erika Puhakka stepped down and President Garrett Edmonds declined to nominate a replacement so close to elections, saying the choice belonged to his successor: "I think that's the only thing that is right in this scenario."
Chief of Staff Lindsey Kelly and enrollment director Donte Reed both resigned in January; Reed was immediately elevated to chief of staff.

patterns.name: Money that cannot be accounted for
patterns.what_it_is: Recurring financial scandal - lost concert money, missing funds, unspent budgets, retroactive bills, conflicts of interest in the scholarships SGA awards itself.
patterns.how_it_changed: In the 1970s the money problem was operational: SGA ran concerts and lost on them ($7,000 in 1975, $3,800 in 1976), and "charges of ASG fund misuse" were aired in the same week the congress created an activities committee. From 2002 it becomes accountability failure - money that vanished into the general fund, purchases with no receipts, a surprise $15,000 bill for a predecessor's contract. By the 2010s the fight shifts to whether SGA members should be able to take SGA's own scholarship money, which the senate twice refused to give up. The 2024 León censure is the mature form: a constitutional clause, a hearing, a vote and a paper trail.

instances.what: An ASG concert drew 4,300 people but lost $7,000. In October charges of ASG fund misuse were heard the same week the congress voted to create an activities committee and a letter writer attacked the organisation. By February the Herald reported financial difficulties might force ASG to drop its entertainment duties.
The Seals and Crofts concert set the Associated Student Government back $3,800; concert finances remained a recurring sore point for the rest of the decade.

"Gazebo-Gate." Members Brooke Smith, Dana Lockhart and Sam Stinson petitioned congress over $28,000 they said was unaccounted for, including about $5,000 set aside in 2001 for a gazebo that was never built. President Jamie Sears said "I have absolutely no idea where that money went." The Herald's eleven-member editorial board called leaders' ignorance "shameful." By October the $13,000 was traced: it had slipped back into the general fund and been spent on other things, including computers for the SGA office.

WKU's Office of the Internal Auditor found $872 in questionable purchases from the SGA Dining Dollars account between August 2003 and May 2004, mostly small buys at campus restaurants with no receipts, and recommended Todd reimburse the money plus $71 for a purchasing-card charge after a spring break car rental. Campus police determined no police action was necessary.

SGA left about $24,000 of its $115,000 budget unspent at the end of 2005-06, money that returned to Western's general fund. Administrative Vice President Amanda Allen called the previous year a bad budgetary year but also a learning year.

SGA paid Parking Services a $15,000 retroactive bill for the previous year's Provide-A-Ride after Parking Services found no record of the prior administration's payment, taking $7,500 each from organizational aid and student scholarships. Billy Stephens said he was "shocked"; Colton Jessie insisted his administration had budgeted the money.

The senate stripped out the bylaw barring serving SGA members from SGA-sponsored scholarships. President Cory Dodds and three colleagues then published a commentary attacking the senate for it, writing that 11 SGA members had received such awards since spring 2011 and calling it a breach of student trust.

Former senator Jody Dahmer published a letter to the editor arguing a precedent set during the past session had damaged the organizational aid process, describing organisations meeting the committee outside the senate with reports then forwarded and voted on quickly.

The Judicial Council censured Administrative Vice President Salvador León 6-0 for spending funds before the Senate authorised them, under the constitution's clause 2.5.3 requiring the AVP to expend funds only as the Senate authorises.

patterns.name: Fighting the Board of Regents
patterns.what_it_is: Direct confrontation with WKU's governing board - over its chairman, its contracts, its fees, its process. The place where SGA's formal representation and its actual power are furthest apart.
patterns.how_it_changed: The pattern is remarkably stable: SGA passes a resolution, the board does what it was going to do. In 1991 the body asked the regents not to re-elect a chairman under federal investigation; they re-elected him a week later. In 2015 it disapproved 21-4 of how the Confucius Institute building was approved; the board declined to revisit and Richey told the senate "it's a done deal, the building will be built." What changes is the student regent's posture: from voting yes under protest (2001) through abstention (2006) to public open letters of dissent (2016) and lone recorded no votes (2026). The dissent gets louder as it stays equally ineffective.

instances.what: Resolution 91-6-F asked that Joe Iracane not be re-elected chair of the Board of Regents, citing that he was under investigation by the FBI, the IRS and U.S. attorneys in Indiana and Kentucky over an alleged $6 million payment to Pyramid Mining Co. in return for contracts, and that he had overstepped into operations reserved for the president under the board's bylaws. It asked student regent Heather Falmlen to vote against him. On 6 November the board re-elected him anyway.

The Board of Regents voted 8-2 to raise the $16 student athletic fee by $40 in January 2001 and another $40 that fall. Student Regent Cassie Martin and Faculty Regent Mary Ellen Miller cast the two votes against; Martin said she questioned the timing and the amount and disagreed with raising fees mid-year.

The board voted on 17 August to raise tuition 9 percent, before fall classes officially began. Student Regent Leslie Bedo told the board the timing sent a message that the university would slide the increase through before students could respond - then joined the unanimous vote approving it.

The board approved the $46-per-semester construction fee 9-1 with Katie Dawson abstaining, and rejected 10-1 her proposal to exempt the following year's seniors. She said she supported the fee but could not vote for it with so many seniors counting on the exemption.

Student regent Jeanne Johnson seconded Louisville regent Larry Zielke's motion to cap the tuition increase at 6 percent and push the General Assembly for more funding; it died with only two votes, and the board approved 9 percent.

The senate voted 21-4 for Resolution 2-15-F disapproving of the nontransparent procedure by which the Model Confucius Institute building was authorized - the contract signed in China in December 2014, the board voting more than a month later without full details disclosed. On 30 September Richey told the senate the board had declined to revisit it: "Just to clarify, it's a done deal, the building will be built." Some senators had warned him the vote would make "powerful enemies."

Student regent Jay Todd Richey published an open letter to students explaining his vote against the board's 6-4-1 approval of a Medical Center partnership, arguing it would tie WKU to a single health care provider for up to 99 years, and writing that although bound to uphold the decision he believed it was a bad deal.

Resolution 3-18-S passed unanimously, seeking renegotiation of the 20-year Aramark contract under which the per-semester dining fee for full-time students without a meal plan would climb from $75 to $150, then $300, then $350 - about $2,800 over four years. President Andi Dahmer said the contract was never brought to SGA or the full Board of Regents.

At the Board of Regents retreat, Student Regent Sam Kurtz raised student-worker funding cuts as units were ordered to cut 7.5 percent of approved spending and absorb a 10 percent overhead charge, asking the room "Isn't that the point of why we're all here, to look out for the students?" He later told the Herald the answers he got were cookie-cutter.

At his last meeting as student regent, Rush Robinson cast the only vote against a $204, 1.69 percent tuition increase - the sixth consecutive yearly rise - saying the board had to do everything it could to preserve affordability. Every other regent voted in favour.

patterns.name: The student regent seat: a twenty-five-year fight for a vote, then a fight over who holds it
patterns.what_it_is: The origin story of SGA's only formal external power, and the long argument about whether that power is real.
patterns.how_it_changed: The seat was created by state legislation reported in committee in February 1968 and filled that April by William Menser - and carried no vote for years. Students were still campaigning for voting power in February 1970 and the Herald was still headlining "Student Regent May Get Vote" in February 1972, four years in. Because it was separately elected, several plaque years carry two names. It merged with the presidency by the 1990s, which made every presidential resignation a governance crisis, and the 2009 split - president and regent held by two different people - had to be resolved by the courts of SGA itself.

instances.what: A Herald article headlined "Ward Favors Student on Board of Regents" reported support for the idea, months before Western sent lobbyists to Frankfort or a bill reached committee.

A bill reached committee on 8 February; the same issue carried students berating dorm rules and a letter headed "Wanted: Work for Judicial Council." On 4 April the Herald reported Menser "assumes duties as Regent Board Member." The seat carried no vote.

Because Associated Students president Bill Straeffer was an out-of-state student, the Congress of Associated Students elected Paul Gerard, a Bowling Green junior, to the seat instead. He sat as a non-voting member.

Two pieces in one February issue: Associated Students seeking voting rights for the student regent, and student and faculty "associate" regents pressing for a vote, with an editorial calling for support of Senate Bill 75. In March the legislature dropped the bill, under a headline that lawmakers had kept students impotent.
"Student Regent May Get Vote" - four years after the seat was created it was still non-voting.

The regents bill changing how the student regent was chosen passed the state House; five students sought the seat in the first campus-wide election for it; no candidate won a majority on 9 February, forcing a runoff Sandra Norfleet won on 16 February. By mid-April the Herald noted her two-month term was nearing its end.
President Margaret Ragan wrote in the Herald to explain that the Associated Student Government presidency and the student regent position were now separate.

Bill #92-01-S proposed a Student Advisory Committee of class presidents, a representative from each college and the executive council to brief the student regent on Board agenda items and canvass student opinion before each meeting.

The Herald corrected a misquotation of President John Bradley: there was a consensus among Kentucky student government presidents that student regents should not vote for tuition increases, but Bradley said he had never personally committed to withholding such a vote.

Boles's resignation split the two offices. Kayla Shelton took the presidency but not the regency; a 2-1 Judicial Council vote, over the sitting executive vice president's written objection, ordered the special election that gave the seat to Reagan Gilley. The Board of Regents administered his oath on 24 April 2009, and the split closed at the summer handover.

patterns.name: Tuition, fees and the annual defeat
patterns.what_it_is: The oldest external fight in the record and the one SGA has never won on its own terms: opposing the price of attending WKU.
patterns.how_it_changed: The instrument changes - a bill in 1977, a cap proposal in 1991, a rally in 1993 and again in 2003, 2004, 2010, 2011, 2016, 2018 and 2024, a lone dissenting vote in 2026 - and the outcome does not. The one clear reversal in the record is negotiated rather than won: in 2009 SGA and university officials agreed to strike a proposed $30 per-credit-hour fee from the Board agenda, replacing it with a rise in the add/drop fee, and SGA cancelled its planned protest. Student Regent Reagan Gilley called it "really a win-win for everyone." Increasingly SGA has argued for fees rather than against them - a $3 radio fee (2003), a $9 Talisman fee (2005), a $30 parking-garage fee (2015), a $5 Herald fee (2019), a $5 sustainability fee (2024).

instances.what: The congress approved Bill 9, formally opposing a proposed tuition increase, in the same March meeting that created a Complaint Committee to handle student grievances.

ASG asked the state to evaluate higher education in a legislative season dominated by budget worries; in April, close ASG races prompted recounts in the same week the Council on Higher Education approved a tuition increase.

In a single February issue, ASG wanted to cap tuition increases, proposed an overhaul of Detrex registration, and planned lobbying to protect financial aid - the broadest policy week of the Colvin year.

About 200 students from six public universities rallied at the Capitol against cuts after the Kentucky House passed a budget cutting Western's funding by more than $1 million. Western sent about 20 people; Sears said 17 "took the initiative to get on the bus."

SGA organized Walk Out Western, asking students to leave class at 12:20 p.m. on 25 October for a rally at the Colonnade, with empty seats meant as a message to Frankfort. President Gary Ransdell said he could not condone students walking out of class and doubted a single-campus protest would affect state funding.
SGA cancelled the $1,175 bus it had planned to run to the Rally for Higher Education, arranging carpools instead, after only eight people confirmed they were attending - about $150 per student.

SGA passed a resolution supporting a $10 million parking garage funded by a $30-per-semester increase. Ransdell had already told SGA that approving even a $4 fee for Student Legal Services would be difficult and that he would be reluctant to take it to the Board.

Student regent Stephen Mayer opposed that year's 4 percent tuition increase and was an outspoken critic of the $450 online academic fee, saying he did not see the need to put the burden "on the students' backs."

Resolution 18-23-S put SGA on record supporting a $50 cap on student parking fees, noting citations ranged from $10 to $600, alongside Bill 19-23-S setting aside $700 to pay citations for financially vulnerable students.
Lucas said before taking the regent seat that he was "generally concerned" by a proposed $210 tuition increase; the board approved $204 days later over Robinson's lone no vote.

patterns.name: The administration overrules the students - and occasionally does not
patterns.what_it_is: The pattern of SGA passing something, the administration declining it, and SGA discovering the limit of a resolution. Includes the rare inverse: the campaigns that worked.
patterns.how_it_changed: Early confrontations were about campus life and rights - dorm inspections, visitation, an Office of Black Affairs. From the 2000s they became academic and contractual, and the pattern hardened into a formula: SGA passes a resolution, an administrator responds by email or letter, the answer is no.
