Ransdell's 2015 email answering four SGA resolutions at once is the purest example of the genre - a president formally replying to student legislation, granting the cheap items and deferring the expensive ones to the Board and the Council on Postsecondary Education. The wins are instructive: they came when SGA supplied a number an administrator could act on (a 1,500-signature petition in 2003, 3,500 signatures in three days in 2020), not when it passed a resolution.

instances.what: The Associated Student Government rejected President Dero Downing's position on an Office of Black Affairs, one of the sharpest confrontations of the fall.

A fall-long fight over dormitory room inspections: a September measure voted down amid criticism of how the vote was conducted, a bill calling for a ban on bugs in the dorms that drew a mocking cartoon, an ASG that nearly slept through its own November vote before re-endorsing inspections, then a bill proposing a stricter room-entry rule.

About fifty students gathered outside the Wetherby Administration Building chanting "It's not your choice. Keep our voice," urging the university to retain the Vice President of Student Affairs and Dean of Student Life positions, after Resolution 99-1-F asked that Jerry Wilder be retained.

SGA fought the plus/minus grading proposal with unanimous legislation, a petition that passed 1,500 signatures, a planned rally and, in Bradley's words, meetings with university donors. In April 2007 Provost Barbara Burch told the University Senate she would not implement the system it had passed 36-23; Jeanne Johnson credited SGA's campaign.

Ransdell told senators that eliminating the two-year on-campus housing requirement did not work "from a business standpoint" because debts remained on dormitory renovations. SGA had been the only campus body to make removal of that requirement a condition of its tobacco-ban resolution; Speaker Kaylee Egerer said she never expected the Regents to enact SGA's version.

After the senate voted 19-8 against renaming Downing University Center, the Administrative Council decided the building would be called Downing Student Union anyway. Former Executive Vice President Kendrick Bryan wrote that Dodds had correctly told campus officials students preferred the old name and that student opinion had not changed.

Administrators changed the winning "Dub the Pub" name from Topper Tavern to Topper Grill and Pub, reflecting Ransdell's wish to downplay the alcohol theme. Richey said he was "very disappointed" and that it made SGA question how much the administration listens to students. Weeks earlier SGA had refused to supply the enforcement corps for the campus smoking phaseout: "SGA has no intention on actually being the group that enforces this."

Ransdell wrote declining Resolution 6-15-F's meningitis vaccination requirement for incoming freshmen, saying the university would highly recommend vaccination but "stop short of requiring it," citing a $143.77 cost for uninsured students.

Housing and Residence Life's 10-year plan made Southwest Hall honors housing and Northeast Hall international housing, with no mention of the integration SGA had endorsed 27-1 the previous October. An SGA Twitter poll had found about 83 percent support for merging the populations.

Associate Provost Rob Hale rebuffed SGA's Pass/D/Fail request, calling the extended drop deadline sufficient; Edmonds said he was "deeply disturbed." His petition drew more than 3,500 signatures in three days and SGA presented nearly 20 pages of student testimony. On 1 December the provost reversed the university's position.

WKU General Counsel Andrea Anderson told the Senate that House Bill 4 applies to SGA because SGA receives university money, that the WKU Pride Center would lose its university-related status and DSU office, and that SGA could still fund organisations only if content neutral - with social media and digital content counting as a resource.

patterns.name: The Herald as adversary, referee and eventually client
patterns.what_it_is: Sixty years of the student newspaper covering, mocking, scolding and being funded by the student government - the longest continuous external relationship in the archive.
patterns.how_it_changed: The paper doubted the organisation before it existed ("We Do Not Deserve Student Government," May 1966) and never stopped. Presidents answered in print - Linda Jones with a formal correction in 1972, Bob Moore disputing an editorial in 1977, Jack Smith writing "Cartoon Aggravates" in 1983, Tim Todd criticising the paper's reporting in 1986. In the 1990s and 2000s the Herald became the auditor: it named Gazebo-Gate, called leaders' ignorance "shameful," documented Andi Dahmer's harassment, and its editorial board repeatedly told SGA it had one job. The relationship inverts in the 2010s: SGA nominates members to the committee that helps choose the Herald's editor (a fight that cost three senators in 2009), backs the paper in its lawsuit against WKU, and in 2019 votes 23-1 to endorse a $5 per-student fee to fund it.

instances.what: The issue reporting Jim Haynes's win as the first president carried a skeptical editorial titled "We Do Not Deserve Student Government."

President Linda Jones wrote a piece headlined "Associated Students Corrects Herald," a public correction of the paper's reporting on the organization. Three days earlier the paper had run "Chaos Reigns at Associated Students Meeting."
The Herald headlined Bob Moore's questioning of freshman campaign spending "A$G?", answered with an editorial that his comment was not good politics, and printed his letter disputing it.
The Herald reported ASG had voided its own procedures, mocked the body with a Lou Bloss cartoon, and printed Jack Smith's letter saying the cartoon aggravated him.
Five days after SGA proposed a skywalk at the bottom of the Hill, the Herald told it to "ditch the pie-in-the-sky idea," and a letter in the same issue called the association a "puppet" group.

Vice president Matthew Bastin circulated a memo of the fall's passed legislation to the SGA advisor, officers, committee heads and the Herald's editor, answering accusations that SGA had been unproductive. The list itself was the rebuttal.

The Herald's eleven-member editorial board attacked SGA over "Gazebo-Gate," calling leaders' ignorance about the missing money "shameful" and challenging Sears by name to "do her job," writing that "I don't know" did not cut it.
A Herald editorial the week of Rob Watkins's resignation was headlined "SGA actions an embarrassment to Western."

Three senators resigned over the president's nomination of Greg Capillo to the Student Publications Committee, which helps choose the Herald's editor-in-chief, with Michel Stephens saying the pick was not based on merit or experience.

A Herald editorial accused SGA of failing students on the priority registration hour cap, saying the executive vice president voted for the policy at University Senate without SGA questioning it first, and that SGA had one job - representing students - and had not done it.

Resolution 5-19-S endorsed a $5 per-student publications fee to support the College Heights Herald, passing 23-1, with Academic and Student Affairs Chair Amanda Harder noting SGA had previously backed the Herald in its ongoing lawsuit against WKU.

patterns.name: Whether SGA is allowed to have opinions about the world
patterns.what_it_is: The recurring constitutional-temperament fight: is student government a service organisation or a political one? It surfaces whenever the senate takes a position beyond the campus fence.
patterns.how_it_changed: The archive itself flags 1969 as the origin - the Associated Student Congress endorsing the Vietnam Moratorium, which the Herald called a bold step, and which the record explicitly ties to the same argument returning in 2017 and 2023. The position has never settled. The senate endorsed a congressional candidate in 1982 and the Herald said endorsing was not wise for ASG; it rejected an MLK holiday in 1986 and split over one in 1987; it failed a clean DREAM Act resolution 12-17 in 2017 on the grounds that it was "not the university's place to put our political hat in a ring," then passed a narrower DACA solidarity resolution 32-1 two weeks later by staying inside "a jurisdiction that we do have." By 2024 the senate voted unanimously to declare itself nonpartisan, and in 2025 it renamed its own diversity committee under a federal executive order.

instances.what: The Associated Student Congress endorsed the Vietnam Moratorium; the Herald called it a bold step. The archive records it as the clearest early example of the body taking a position outside the campus fence - "the same argument that returns in 2017 and 2023."
ASG backed William Natcher; five days later the paper editorialized that endorsing was not wise for ASG.
ASG rejected a proposal to dismiss classes for the Martin Luther King holiday in January 1986. A Martin Luther King bill passed the following March with members split by the argument.
SGA passed a measure calling for gays to be included in Western's anti-discrimination policy by a slim margin, a week after covering the proposal's introduction.

Resolution 6-17-S, supporting reparations for Black students, passed 19-10-1 and drew national wire coverage, a Tucker Carlson interview and fabricated headlines claiming WKU had granted free tuition. Ransdell stated within days that it was not a university position. Both authors described it as a conversation starter. The same year the senate stripped "reparations" language out of its own resolution on qualities for WKU's tenth president, changing it to "restitution" and then removing it entirely.

Resolution 2-17-F urging a clean DREAM Act failed 12-17, Senator Alex Sergent saying it was not the university's place to "put our political hat in a ring" and William Hurst saying "we serve the majority." Two weeks later a rewritten resolution declaring solidarity with WKU's own DACA students passed 32-1.
Resolution 7.21f, condemning the banning of critical race theory teaching in postsecondary education, passed 16-15 with two abstentions after weeks of debate.

The student advocacy group "For the People" told the Senate SGA was the only major organization not to oppose Turning Point USA bringing Kyle Rittenhouse to campus. Kurtz replied that as an apolitical organization SGA's role was to ensure all voices could be heard. The same night senators voted on 13 constitutional amendments. In September Bill 50-23-S, reaffirming SGA as nonpartisan and stating its duty to put forward only nonpartisan legislation, passed unanimously.
Robinson ran on turning SGA away from national politics toward direct student advocacy, saying the organization had sometimes echoed national talking points.

patterns.name: Who is actually in the room: Greek dominance and factional capture
patterns.what_it_is: A recurring charge that the body is captured by a small slice of campus, raised with the same numbers across five decades.
patterns.how_it_changed: In the 1970s the Herald simply reported it as fact - a primary that "showed Greek influence," Greeks "continuing to dominate the campus political scene." In 2011 the Herald quantified it: 21 of 50 members Greek, more than 40 percent, against under 8 percent campus-wide, with two fraternities accounting for nine of them, and an administrative vice president handing his post to his Lambda Chi Alpha "little brother." In 2018 a Greek member of SGA tried to defund Greek councils and lost by one vote, citing the University of Alabama's Machine. In 2024 an outside student group put the figure at 40 percent again. The number does not move; the argument gets more explicit each time.

instances.what: Jeff Consolo and Steve Henry won the spring election in a cycle whose primary the Herald said showed Greek influence.
Reporting Steve Henry's election, the paper noted that Greeks continued to dominate the campus political scene.

The Herald reported 21 of SGA's 50 members belonged to Greek organizations, more than 40 percent, while less than 8 percent of the student body was; sixteen of the 21 were fraternity men, and Sigma Chi and Lambda Chi Alpha accounted for nine. Weeks later Administrative Vice President Wade Pierce, who chaired the organizational aid committee, said he would be succeeded by Devon Hilderbrandt, his committee co-chair and his "little brother" in Lambda Chi Alpha, who ran unopposed.

Bill 10-18-F, barring SGA funding to Interfraternity and Panhellenic Council chapters, was defeated 16-17. Author Amy Wyer, herself a member of Alpha Gamma Delta, cited the University of Alabama's Machine and said only one non-Greek member had been elected to that student government since 1914: "I fear we have the potential to move in this direction." In January the senate had postponed confirming Stephen Mayer to a vacant seat after Will Hurst called the nomination of "another fraternity man" hypocritical.

A motion to cancel the 8 October senate meeting for Kappa Delta's Shenanigans philanthropy event passed 17-15; Senator Anthony Survance argued that given recent Greek controversies SGA should not signal endorsement, and later said the vote helped prompt the protest he and Symone Whalin organised at the event.

Avery Wells and the student group "For the People" told the Senate that 40 percent of the Senate belonged to Greek life and that SGA had a disconnect with cultural communities on campus. Kurtz replied that he did not control who chose to run.

patterns.name: Internal harassment and the year the conflict left the building
patterns.what_it_is: Factional hostility escalating past procedure into personal harassment, culminating in the only episode in the record that produced federal litigation against the university.
patterns.how_it_changed: This is the newest of the patterns and has no clear pre-2016 analogue in the archive. It begins as complaints the organisation cannot process - a racism complaint in 2016 whose investigation was nullified when the two accused resigned, with SGA never releasing their identities or the alleged remarks - and reaches its extreme in 2017-18, when the president described the year as "almost toxic in nature" and the outgoing executive vice president called it "absolute hell." The Dahmer case then did something no other internal SGA fight has done: it moved into federal court and stayed there for six years, forcing the university president to convene a review of WKU's Title IX and Student Conduct processes.

instances.what: After Chief Justice Cody Cox told the senate he had received a complaint that several SGA members made racist remarks, senator Braxton Powell and justice John McKinney resigned the next morning citing scheduling conflicts and personal reasons. The Judicial Council's planned investigation was dropped because the students had already left SGA, and the organization never released the identities of the accused or the nature of the alleged remarks.

Andi Dahmer told the Herald that SGA members cursed at her and called her derogatory names, that a GroupMe thread of eight people called the "Justice Friends" wished her physical harm, and that a profane note left on her car on 9 February led her to file a police report and avoid her residence hall for two weeks: "That's when I really started fearing for my life on this campus." The Title IX office found the conduct did not meet the legal standard; the Office of Student Conduct issued no-contact orders against two senators. She did not seek re-election, citing a year "almost toxic in nature" and partisan ideology in a nonpartisan body.

In their final officer reports, Executive Vice President Savannah Molyneaux called the year "awful" and an "absolute hell," said sexism and misogyny persisted in the senate, and cited the threatening note and the derogatory names used in the SGA offices. Director of Public Relations Amy Wyer disclosed she had become "a statistic, a victim and a survivor" during the year. President Timothy Caboni convened a faculty-staff-student committee to review WKU's Title IX, EEO and Student Conduct processes.
U.S. District Judge David Hale granted the defendants summary judgment, finding WKU had not been deliberately indifferent and the incidents not severe enough to constitute actionable harassment.

The Sixth Circuit vacated summary judgment on the pre-February 2018 Title IX student-on-student harassment claims and vacated qualified immunity for SGA faculty adviser Charley Pride, while upholding dismissal of the retaliation claim over Caboni declining to write a Rhodes Scholarship recommendation.
The parties settled in January, with WKU's insurance carrier paying Dahmer $10,000 and the university's attorney describing the payment as nominal and made without any admission of wrongdoing.

patterns.name: Turnout and the apathy argument that never ends
patterns.what_it_is: Not a fight between factions but the fight the organisation has with the student body, present from the first month of its existence and never resolved.
patterns.how_it_changed: It does not change, which is the finding. The 1966 constitutional referendum drew 2,538 votes - "a larger raw turnout than most SGA elections have managed since" - out of an enrollment of roughly 8,500. The 1968 election drew 2,894, about 34 percent. By 1976 a presidential primary drew 527 ballots; by 1979 a primary drew 830 and the Herald had shifted from scolding non-voters to publishing a defence of not voting. The 2004 constitution that made every student a member was ratified by 132 of about 18,000. The one thing that reliably moves turnout is contest: 2,442 voted in Richey's contested 2016 re-election, one of the highest in the association's history; 908 voted in 2014, down 555; the 2023, 2024 and 2025 presidencies were won on unopposed tickets; and in 2026, with a genuine two-way race, 1,601 voted, 635 more than the year before - what the archive itself calls the clearest evidence in the whole record that WKU turnout tracks whether there is an actual contest.

instances.what: Students ratified the constitution 1,812 to 726 in a four-day referendum; 2,538 students voted, a larger raw turnout than most SGA elections have managed since.

Straeffer beat Whitley 1,732 to 1,098; total turnout was 2,894 votes, about 34 percent of the roughly 8,500-student enrollment. The Herald ran an editorial in the same issue headed "Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference."
With filing open for the spring elections, the Herald reported twenty student government offices going begging for candidates.
The spring primary drew 830 voters. The same issue carried a piece justifying student apathy in ASG voting - the paper had moved from scolding non-voters to explaining them.
Whitehouse emerged from a field of seven for president in a year when only two of 32 congress positions were contested.

Candidates withdrew from the ASG races, saving a primary that would otherwise have been invalid; only two candidates were running for president, illustrated by a cartoon of student government in an empty room.

A Herald editorial criticized student participation after only 132 of about 18,000 students voted on SGA's new constitution, contrasting that with the 86 percent who voted in South Africa's 1999 general elections.
Turnout fell to 908, down 555 votes from the previous year. A Herald editorial called turnout below 1,000 pathetic.
Richey was re-elected with 64 percent in one of the highest-turnout elections in the association's history, 2,442 voters.
Bornefeld reported the fall election vote total rose from 398 the previous fall to 805.
1,601 students voted in a contested race, 635 more than the year before - a 66 percent jump. The three preceding presidential elections had been won on unopposed tickets.

notes:
WHERE THE ARCHIVE IS THIN, AND WHAT THAT DOES TO THE FINDINGS.

1. The pre-1992 record is Herald-shaped, and mostly headline-shaped. For roughly the first twenty-five years the evidence is a digitised Herald article index, not article text. The file says so repeatedly and explicitly: "The archive does not yet hold the text of either article, only their headlines" (1968, Menser's head fee and the ASG retrospective); "The archive does not yet hold the article's text, so the underlying dispute is not yet confirmed" (1972, the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union court action involving Associated Students and The Fly); "The archive does not yet hold the article's text or what it corrected" (1972, Linda Jones correcting the Herald); "The archive does not yet hold the article's text, only its headline crediting his administration with a single major accomplishment" (1974, Yater). This means every pre-1992 internal conflict in my patterns is a conflict the Herald chose to headline. Quiet censures, private resignations, committee-level fights and any dispute the paper did not name are structurally invisible. The 1970s and 1980s look less litigious than the 2010s partly because the 2010s have minutes and the 1970s have headlines.

2. Specific dead years. 1979-80 (Hargrove) is the emptiest presidency in the file: "The archive does not yet show what Hargrove's administration passed or fought over during 1979-80 beyond the record's general sweep of the year." The 1987-88 presidential result is unrecorded - the Herald endorsed Greg Elder, indexed the race as "no contest," and "the indexed issues that survive do not record the published result"; Todd is carried through 1988 only by a two-year plaque plate. 1990-91 ends with "The archive does not preserve further detail of how the term ended." 1992-93 has minutes but "no full officer list, committee structure, or seat count survives beyond the president." 1995-96 and several 1990s years have no senate roster at all. 2002-03's full-text minutes "sit behind an automated-access check and have not been read."

3. The impeachment gap is real and large. Between the Faulk acquittal in April 1976 and the articles drafted against Nick Todd in April 2004 there is no impeachment proceeding anywhere in this file - twenty-eight years. There is also no documented censure before 2015. I do not think this means none occurred; the 1980s produced recounts (1981), a voided general election (1982), a revote (1984) and a write-in dispute that lasted six months (1988), which is not the profile of an organisation with no disciplinary conflict. It means the disciplinary record only becomes visible when SGA starts keeping and posting its own minutes.

4. The Judicial Council's first decade is nearly blank. The council existed from the start - a February 1968 letter headed "Wanted: Work for Judicial Council," Bill Martin's column questioning its work that same month, and a December 1968 report that it had begun hearing student cases. Then nothing until it denies Ed Johnson's election appeal in April 1978. Ten years of a judicial branch with three headlines.

5. Vetoes are almost certainly undercounted before 2004. The archive records a 1981 veto, a 1991 by-law rewrite of the override procedure (Bill #91-6-S) that was tested within weeks, and one unattributed vetoed resolution in 1996. A body that bothered to amend its override procedure in 1991 was presumably using the veto; the file does not show it.

6. Two structural cautions on the evidence I used. First, the plaque this archive is built around is unreliable in ways the file flags itself - Zielke's term is recorded a year late and wrongly paired with Lyne; Kayla Shelton's "2009" plate was filed against the wrong year; Todd, Smith and Gerard sit on multi-year plates that may compress separate terms. I dated conflicts to events, not plates. Second, the identity of some figures is inferred rather than documented: "Amanda Lich" on the plaque against Amanda Coates in every contemporaneous source; Christy Mollozzi against Christy Vogt; Nicki Seay and Nicki Taylor, which the file establishes as one continuous officeholder who changed her surname mid-term rather than a succession.

7. One conflict type I looked for and did not find enough of to report as a pattern: fights with the city of Bowling Green. The record has ASG resolving to fight the noise ordinance and sending officers to a city meeting in 1991, a 1973 recycling-ordinance dispute that "left ASG holding the bag," a 1977 fight over a beer licence for a local pizzeria, a 2017 resolution backing a Fairness Ordinance the city commission had failed to pass, and a 2021 vendor-vetting bill after a Lost River Pizza post. That is a thread, not a pattern - four decades apart with nothing connecting them.

8. Finally, a note on what "external" means here. The single most consequential external fight in the file is not a fight SGA chose: Andi Dahmer's 2018-2024 litigation began as an internal harassment problem and became a federal case against WKU, its president, its assistant general counsel and SGA's own faculty adviser. It is the only instance in sixty-one years where an SGA dispute produced a court order compelling the university to do something.

seam: The standing business of WKU's student government is not policy so much as friction: for sixty years the same short list of grievances — getting across campus, paying for books, being safe at night, being fed, being graded fairly, being housed decently, being heard in Frankfort — comes back every four or five years wearing whatever clothes the decade supplies. What changes is not the subject but SGA's position in relation to it. In the first thirty years SGA asks the university to do things: put a phone there, open the library later, run a shuttle, hire someone to administer scholarships (Resolution 79-10, 1979). In the last thirty it increasingly does them itself, out of its own budget: $600 a year to keep Helm-Cravens open until 2 a.m., $15,000 a year for a safe ride van, $23,500 in scholarships, 450 Uber vouchers, 15 borrowable calculators, $10,000 split among 33 clubs. The organisation converts from petitioner to small vendor of student services. The second seam runs the other way: as the offices merged and the student regent became the SGA president (separately elected 1968-1982, merged by the 1990s), the same person who passes the resolution against a tuition increase now has to sit on the board that votes it — Cassie Martin dissenting 8-2 on the athletics fee in 2000, Katie Dawson abstaining on the $46 construction fee in 2006, Jeanne Johnson seconding a dead motion to cap at 6 percent in 2008, Rush Robinson casting the lone no on $204 in 2026. And a third seam, the oldest: the Herald has been publishing the same editorial about apathy since 27 October 1966.

patterns.name: Campus safety, lighting and getting students home at night
patterns.what_it_is: Lighting, crosswalks, emergency phones, escorts and safe rides — the single most continuous service line in the archive, and the one where SGA moved furthest from asking to operating.
patterns.span: 1983-2026 (43 years documented; nothing on lighting or night safety appears in the archive before 1983)
patterns.how_it_changed: The 1980s ask is a resolution asking the university to install something — a light, a crosswalk, window screens. The 1990s ask is hardware SGA lobbies for and then counts: blue-light emergency phones, one and two at a time, plus a skywalk the Herald told them to ditch. From 1996 SGA stops asking and starts running the service itself, buying a van; by 2011 that costs it a surprise $15,000 retroactive bill and by 2017 Uber has eaten the ridership (5,000 riders in fall 2015 down to nearly 1,500 in fall 2016). The 2020s answer is to subsidise the commercial service instead — $10 Uber vouchers — and go back to crosswalks, which is where the 1987 congress started.

instances.what: Herald's opening issue reports the student escort service will resume, alongside a floated discount card.
Student government defeats a campus lighting proposal in the last week of the fall semester — one of the few outright defeats of legislation reported that year.
Congress passes a crosswalk resolution; campus safety items including new screens for dormitory windows fill much of the fall agenda.
Bill 93-6-F proposes purchasing and installing emergency telephones on campus; the Herald is still reporting on SGA's security phones the following February.

'New Security Phone, Shuttle Stop, Trees Lead to Student Government's To Do List' — in the same issue reporting a mystery caller scaring students with stalking and harassment. Two more emergency phones go in that August. Candidate Tara Higdon's own experience of being stalked shapes the spring campaign.
SGA proposes a skywalk at the bottom of the Hill; five days later the Herald tells it to 'ditch the pie-in-the-sky idea.' In October it proposes more campus lighting.
'Kristen Miller Makes Plan to Drive Party-Goers Home' — the origin of Provide-A-Ride.
A crosswalk on Dogwood Drive; Bill 97-3-F funds designated driver cards.
Resolution 98-7-F asks that University Boulevard be widened with a pedestrian traffic island. It fails.
Provide-A-Ride runs as a free service, Thursday and Friday 11 p.m. to 2 a.m., a fifteen-passenger blue van answering calls within about fifteen minutes; all a rider needs is a valid Western ID.
929 riders over twelve nights, September 20 to November 9, nightly counts from 49 to 112.

Campus improvements chair Shawn Peavie announces SGA is looking into a campus safety commission to test everything from checking locks to recording emergency response times; Bradley had sat on the Campus Safety Task Force formed after the death of freshman Katie Autry.
Smiley urges senators to join the Campus Safety Walk, looking for dimly lit or overgrown areas of campus.
SGA pays Parking Services a surprise $15,000 retroactive Provide-A-Ride bill, $7,500 each from organizational aid and scholarships.
Bill 10-15-S allocates $825.95 for a surveillance camera near the DSU ATMs, passing 15-5.
The RAVE Guardian campus safety app is introduced; in November SGA launches SafeWalk, a call line pairing students who feel unsafe with student escorts.
Safe Ride's Purple Line loses Thursday service as ridership falls to about one rider an hour; Richey blames Uber's arrival in Bowling Green.
Three crosswalk resolutions pass unanimously in one night — below the Van Meter green space, in front of 1600 Chestnut St. and near 1566 Normal St.
450 Uber vouchers worth $10 each, distributed by giveaway, meeting attendance and need-based scholarship.
Resolution 7-26-S backs a crosswalk at Alumni Avenue and Kentucky Street, arguing residents of 1355 Kentucky Street must 'step into oncoming traffic' to reach the Alumni Square garage.

patterns.name: Parking, the shuttle and getting around campus
patterns.what_it_is: Fees, spaces, routes, shelters and fines. Runs the whole sixty years and is the clearest register of the campus physically outgrowing itself.
patterns.how_it_changed: In 1972 students question a $5 vehicle registration fee. In 1983 they vote — 206 of them — for the idea of a shuttle at all. By 1991 the shuttle exists and the fight is over its $10 fare, called 'outrageous and unfair' to infrequent riders. By 2015 SGA is voting to raise its own tuition $30 a semester to build a $10 million garage. By 2024 it is capping the fines and paying them for students who cannot, and by 2026 it is being told the buses' diesel bill has doubled from seven or eight thousand dollars a month to fourteen. The arc runs from resenting a fee, to asking for a service, to funding the service, to absorbing its costs.

instances.what: The regents approve a five dollar vehicle registration fee; the same issue reports students questioning it.
Jeff Consolo's term credited with 'gaining parking board input' alongside cutting bookstore prices.
The outgoing Thornton administration approves resolutions on campus housing and parking policy in its final week; the previous fall's constitution revision came alongside parking rezoning.
ASG floats a shuttle service; 206 students vote for it the following week.
The congress discusses a shuttle from campus to the mall.
SGA seeks shelters and seats for campus shuttle stops.
Resolution 91-2-F asks for a one-way fare option on the Big Red Shuttle, calling the existing $10 fee 'outrageous and unfair' to those who do not ride daily.
Expanded Big Red Shuttle service, a route SGA pushed to extend, draws enthusiasm from local stores along the new stops.
A November flood of resolutions includes a speed hump for the Regents Avenue lot and fifteen-minute parking spaces.

President Leslie Bedo attacks the university after the Forest Park Trailer Park purchase collapses: regents raised the athletics fee expecting 400 to 500 new spaces while Diddle's renovation removed about 200, and she notes more students park on campus than attend basketball games.
A resolution asks WKU to change the policy giving Hilltopper Athletic Foundation donors student parking spaces, including the Grise Hall lot, at basketball games.
$8,000 legislation for a shuttle bus shelter at the Jones-Jaggers stop.
A commuter focus group brings back the idea of an iWKU app function listing each lot's available spaces, plus a South Campus park and ride.
SGA passes a resolution backing a roughly 500-car, $10 million parking structure on part of Creason Lot funded by a $30-per-semester tuition increase.

Resolution 18-23-S supports capping student parking fees at $50, noting citations range from $10 to $600; Bill 19-23-S sets aside $700 to pay citations for financially vulnerable students. Resolution 2132-S seeks awnings or benches at Topper Transit stops.
Parking director tells the 25th Senate's final meeting the monthly diesel bill for WKU buses, normally seven to eight thousand dollars, hit fourteen thousand the previous month.

patterns.name: Textbooks and what they cost
patterns.what_it_is: Book swaps, exchanges, subsidies and the bookstore. One of the two oldest continuous service ideas in the record, and the one that has been reinvented in every available technology.
patterns.how_it_changed: The same idea recurs in the medium of its moment: a physical book swap (1968), an SGA-run exchange (1973, 1975, 1984), a bulletin board in Grise Hall (1991), a dot-com link on the SGA website (Bookswap.com 1998, VarsityBooks.com 1999), a cash subsidy matched by the bookstore (2005, 2008), a pair of iPads loaded with textbooks (2011), a shelf of used Colonnade texts in the SGA office (2018, tabled), and finally an inclusive-access program whose opt-out default SGA interrogates (2022). The grievance is unchanged; the object keeps changing shape.

instances.what: The Herald reports the Associated Student Government directing a student book swap, in the same issue that questions its Judicial Council.
ASG sponsors a student book exchange; the same issue reports a city recycling ordinance has left ASG holding the bag on trash collection for its paper-recycling program.

A spring semester book exchange co-sponsored by ASG and Veterans on Campus; the year's Herald supplement lists it among the Henry administration's wins, alongside ASG being credited with cutting bookstore prices.
The congress begins studying a student book exchange, which becomes the signature project of Jack Smith's final year; by January 1985 the venture looks likely to pause for the summer.
Bill #91-9-S proposes a book exchange bulletin board in Grise Hall.
Bill 98-12-F has SGA sponsor Bookswap.com — an early attempt to use the web against textbook prices.
Bill 99-17-F joins VarsityBooks.com and posts a link from the SGA website, the first e-commerce deal in the digitised SGA record.
SGA passes legislation 22-2 allocating $2,000 to Buy-A-Book, matched by the University Bookstore, amended unanimously to help 20 students instead of 10, chosen by essay and need.
Bill 11-06-F collects textbooks the university bookstore will not buy back and sends them to Africa.

Boles tells the governor's College Access Work Group textbooks average $800 a year; the senate votes $500 to start a Textbook Subsidy Program with $500 matched by the bookstore, and creates a program board of nearly 20.
SGA gives the Educational Resource Center two first-generation iPads to load textbooks onto and lend out free.
Bill 18-18-F, $1,000 for a used-textbook library for Colonnade courses in the SGA offices, is tabled 24-3; Senator Amy Wyer asks why the WKU Bookstore is 'making us buy books they can't resell.'

SGA presses Jennifer Tougas on the Big Red Backpack program's opt-out default; she acknowledges 'schools that use the opt-in approach are far more successful' but says WKU chose opt-out to keep the per-credit-hour cost low.
The senate passes legislation funding textbooks, exam supplies and lab goggles in a single meeting.

patterns.name: Housing and the residence halls
patterns.what_it_is: Who may be in the building, what is in the building, who the building is for, and finally whether the building should still be standing.
patterns.how_it_changed: Three distinct eras. Rules (1968-1985): women's dormitory rules, curfews, visitation, coed halls, the door-ajar rule, room inspections — a decade and a half of arguing about supervision, culminating in a Mass Action Committee strike call over visitation in 1972 and women's hours abolished with ASG's backing by 1976. Amenities (1983-2005): cable, change machines, ice machines, soap and sanitary restrooms, chains so Pearce-Ford Tower windows would open, sprinklers, holiday housing. Then belonging and fabric (2011-2026): the two-year live-on requirement as a bargaining chip against a tobacco ban, integrating honors and international students, LGBTQ-friendly roommate questions, mold, HVAC failures, and buildings scheduled for demolition.

instances.what: A committee investigating women's dormitory rules runs in the same Herald issue as the tuition increase and the student-regent lobbying; students berate dorm rules a fortnight earlier.
ASG urges an investigation of student housing — one of the fall's most pointed challenges to university policy.
The Associated Student Congress passes a resolution on the women's curfew; the Herald reports abolition is unlikely that year and editorialises that the curfew is obsolete.
A Mass Action Committee calls for a strike over dorm visitation in the same issue that installs next year's officers.
An ASG housing survey urges improvement in dormitory conditions.
ASG and the Interhall Council back a coed dorm and abolition of the door-ajar visitation rule.
ASG rejects a move to close Diddle Hall dormitory, amid a fall of housing debates including a push to make Keen Hall coed.

A fall-long fight over dormitory room inspections: a September measure voted down, a bill calling for a ban on bugs in the dorms that drew a cockroach cartoon, a November re-endorsement the Herald says ASG nearly slept through, and a bill for a stricter room-entry rule.
Resolution 80-32 requests change machines in residence halls.
ASG approves a coed housing bill, built through the fall on a joint poll with the Interhall Council.
The congress asks for chains on Pearce-Ford Tower windows so they can be opened; in 1990 it is still asking for those windows to be opened.
The Executive Council writes to four administrators under Resolution 93-18-F asking the university to address housing for students during holiday breaks.
Resolutions on ice machines, soap and sanitary restrooms in residence halls; 1998 brings a push for dorm sprinklers.

SGA passes the tobacco-free resolution 'if and only if' the two-year on-campus living requirement goes; Ransdell tells senators eliminating it does not work 'from a business standpoint' because debts remain on dormitory renovations.

A resolution asks Housing and Residence Life to integrate honors and international students across Southwest and Northeast halls rather than segregating them; it passes 27-1 and is then omitted from HRL's 10-year plan.

The senate votes 28-2 to make the sexual orientation and gender identity question optional on housing applications and add a question asking whether an applicant is comfortable rooming with an LGBTQ student, noting WKU stands at 2 out of 5 on the Campus Pride Index.
Executive Vice President Me'Lon Craighead tells the senate SGA is working with Housing and Residence Life on mold accumulation in residence halls.

Robinson opens the year on Pearce-Ford Tower's HVAC — 29 of more than 600 residents chose to relocate to Hugh Poland. Caboni tells the senate all community showers and bathrooms will be phased out and Hilltopper, McCormick and Rodes Harlin replaced by fall 2030.

Senators learn the legislature has approved the Gilbane partnership to replace Douglas Keen and Hugh Poland; Robinson tells the Faculty Senate to 'take a field trip' and see the state of the residence halls.

patterns.name: Tuition, fees and the road to Frankfort
patterns.what_it_is: Opposing increases, lobbying the state, and — after the offices merged — voting on the increase itself.
patterns.how_it_changed: The 1970s and 80s form is a resolution: Bill 9 opposing a tuition increase (1977), asking the state to evaluate higher education (1981). The 1990s add the bus: a rally at the Capitol that earns Joe Rains a University Senate commendation (1992). The 2000s industrialise it — 200 students from six universities, 47 reserved seats, $650 for transportation, slogans about not balancing the budget on our backs — and then start to doubt it: by 2007 chief of staff Skylar Jordan says 'the traditional February rally had not worked' and builds Listen Up Legislators for one-on-one meetings instead. In 2012 the bus is cancelled when eight people sign up. Meanwhile the president is now the student regent, so the same person opposing the increase has to vote on it, usually alone.

instances.what: Bill 9 formally opposes a proposed tuition increase; the same March meeting creates a Complaint Committee for student grievances.

ASG asks the state to evaluate higher education in a legislative season dominated by budget worries; that autumn it rallies for higher-education funding and then vetoes a plan to pay an education lobbyist.
In one February issue ASG moves to cap tuition increases, proposes overhauling the Detrex registration system, and plans lobbying to protect student financial aid.
The WKU University Senate adopts Resolution R92.11 commending SGA president Joe Rains for taking part in a Frankfort rally against cuts to higher-education funding.
The Board of Regents votes 8-2 to raise the student athletic fee by $80 in two installments; Student Regent Cassie Martin and Faculty Regent Mary Ellen Miller are the two dissenters.

Bedo tells the board an August vote sends 'a message to students' that a 9 percent increase would pass before they could weigh in — in-state tuition from $1,422 to $1,560 — then joins the unanimous vote for it.
About 200 students from six public universities rally at the Capitol; Sears says 17 people 'took the initiative to get on the bus.'

Congress approves $650 for transportation and reserves 47 spots for a February 5 rally under slogans like 'Don't Balance the Budget on Our Backs'; weeks later SGA's own budget is frozen as WKU absorbs $5.6 million in ordered cuts.
Regents approve a $46-per-semester construction fee 9-1 with Dawson abstaining, and reject her proposal to exempt next year's seniors 10-1.
A resolution demands more state funding after WKU received 54 percent of its recommended increase; SGA runs Walk Out Western, an October class walkout Ransdell says he cannot condone.
Student regent Jeanne Johnson seconds Larry Zielke's motion to cap the tuition increase at 6 percent and push the General Assembly instead; it dies with two votes.
SGA cancels its $1,175 bus to the Frankfort rally after eight people confirm, and arranges carpools instead.
Boka organises 'Rally for Retention' in response to a $1.8 million state cut, with speeches and one-on-one meetings with legislators.

Resolution 2-16-S opposes Senate Bill 75's four-year tuition freeze; senators lobby eight state officials in Frankfort, citing about 15,000 students denied need-based aid. Richey, as chair of the Board of Student Body Presidents of Kentucky, co-signs a letter with nine other campuses demanding restoration of the 'Powerball Promise.'
Robinson casts the lone vote against a $204, 1.69 percent increase — the sixth consecutive yearly rise — saying the board has 'to do whatever we can to not raise the tuition.'

patterns.name: Scholarships and organisational aid
patterns.what_it_is: Money out the door: grants to student groups and scholarships to individual students. Now the single largest line in the SGA budget and the thing the organisation most reliably points to when asked what it does.
patterns.how_it_changed: It begins as a request that someone else do it — Resolution 79-10 urging the university to assign staff to administer academic scholarships. By the mid-2000s SGA is the granting body, and the categories track exactly who campus has decided it has been neglecting: study abroad and winter term (2010), students with disabilities (2016), Jonesville and Black students (2016), first-generation students (2018), ISEC and international book scholarships (2022), transfer students (2026). Demand has outrun the pattern: from roughly 40 applications a year to 398 in 2019 and 295 in a single spring in 2025.

instances.what: Resolution 79-10 urges the university to assign staff to administer academic scholarships.
A late-November run of legislation includes child care grants for non-traditional students.

Administrative Vice President Amanda Allen reports $30,000 in organizational aid for the year; that October she adds almost $10,000 more to it after $24,000 of the prior year's $115,000 budget went unspent and returned to WKU's general fund.

SGA raises its scholarship budget from $12,000 to $20,000 and lowers general senate funding from $20,000 to $12,000, capping study abroad awards at $500 a semester and $250 for winter or summer so more students can receive money. Jessie's year ends with the scholarship fund up $8,000 and organizational aid at $40,000.
SGA distributes around $34,000 in organizational aid to about 50 organisations at a $500 maximum each.
The summer and winter need-based scholarship programme is expanded from $6,000 to $21,000, funded in part by an anonymous donation.

Bill 4-16-F creates SGA's first scholarships for students with disabilities, passing unanimously after sophomore Brendan Ward tells senators his ADHD and dyslexia cost him merit scholarships. In November $750 plus $100 creates the Jonesville Memorial Scholarship.

A $1,200 first-generation scholarship in February; in October a recurring $2,000 first-generation scholarship passes 31-1, the Herald citing a WKU Fact Book estimate that 34.8 percent of fall 2016 first-time students were first-generation.
A record 398 scholarship applications: 132 winter term, 122 first-generation, 81 study abroad, 31 scholar development, 10 ISEC, 22 for the revived Earn-a-Computer programme.
$15,500 across five scholarship programmes including a first-ever $500 for Black Student Alliance scholarships, plus $8,000 in organizational aid at $500 per applicant.
A $100,000 budget with $20,000 for organizational aid and $23,500 for scholarships; Kurtz credits Caboni with keeping the total untouched for several years.
295 spring scholarship applications against an average of about 40 in past years; organizational aid graded from 78 applications, with a $50 minimum even for the lowest graded.
$10,000 split among 33 groups in grants of $100 to $500; at year's end every scholarship offered has been awarded and $100 of organizational aid is held back as a reserve for groups in need.

patterns.name: Grading systems
patterns.what_it_is: The scale itself, and the mechanics around it — incompletes, the withdrawal deadline, retaking C grades, plus/minus, value-added, pass/fail.
patterns.how_it_changed: Early legislation is procedural and small: the deadline for incomplete grades (1983), a grade before the 'W' period closes so students can decide whether to drop (1994), reinstating the ten-point scale (1997). Then from 2003 the whole category becomes a defensive war: three separate administrations fight plus/minus grading, and each time the proposal comes back under a new name. SGA wins it in 2007 when Provost Burch declines to implement a system the University Senate had already passed 36-23. In 2020 the polarity flips entirely — instead of resisting a grading change, SGA campaigns for one, and wins Pass/D/Fail with a petition that drew more than 3,500 signatures in three days.

instances.what: ASG passes its proposal on the deadline for incomplete grades after tabling it the week before; the grade plan itself passes that November.
ASG's proposal for a new grade scale is denied, the first setback of the fall.

Resolution 94-11-F asks that students receive a grade before the end of the withdrawal 'W' period so they can make an informed decision about dropping. A proposal to let students retake C grades is killed in committee the same year.
Resolution 97-6-F calls for reinstatement of the ten-point grade scale — 'the grading fight would run on for years at WKU.'

SGA unanimously passes legislation against economics professor Brian Strow's plus/minus proposal; Bradley says he will use every tool including a rally and meetings with university donors; the petition passes 1,500 signatures by November.

Provost Barbara Burch tells the University Senate she will not implement the plus/minus system it passed 36-23; Jeanne Johnson says SGA raised awareness and led student protests and that students would keep fighting if it returned.

Provost Emslie pitches 'value-added' grading — an extra quality point for the top third of B and C grades — telling SGA an earlier plus-minus proposal took years to develop 'only to be dashed at the last minute.' The senate rejects it in a close vote in February 2013.
Hannah Garland's plus-minus resolution is tabled twice, with Dodds floating putting the question directly to students on the spring ballot.

After Associate Provost Rob Hale rebuffs SGA's Pass/D/Fail request, Edmonds's petition passes 3,000 then 3,500 signatures in three days; on December 1 the provost relents and students may take a pass instead of a B or C.

patterns.name: Library hours
patterns.what_it_is: Keeping the library and study space open later, especially at finals.
patterns.how_it_changed: It starts as a request to the administration (1986 proposals, 1989 correspondence between Amos Gott and administrators Bailey, Strickler and Binder). From 1999 SGA simply pays for it — $600 a year, described by 2011 as 'an annual practice,' covering extra staff time and lighting to keep Helm-Cravens open until 2 a.m. from Sunday to Thursday of finals week. By 2025 the ask has escalated to 24/7 hours at the Commons at Helm, and the answer comes back that staffing makes it unworkable and student use would not justify the cost — with the Faculty Senate endorsing 'finding an alternative 24-hour space instead,' because WKU offers none.

instances.what: ASG proposals ask for more library hours, in the same issue that pushes the spring elections back a week.
Extended library hours pursued through signed correspondence between President Amos Gott and administrators Howard Bailey, Sally Ann Strickler and Michael Binder.
Legislation to open the Downing University Center computer lab during finals.
A bill extends library hours during finals week, passed the same day as the VarsityBooks.com deal.
The senate approves $600 to keep the library open until 2 a.m. during finals week; Jessie says continuing the service was never in question, calling finals 'an important time for students.'
$600 to Helm-Cravens for 2 a.m. closing Sunday through Thursday of finals week — 'an annual practice.'
Bill 15-16-S allocates $600 for the same purpose at the year's final meeting.

Resolution 1-25-S seeks 24/7 hours at the Commons at Helm during finals week, noting WKU offers no 24-hour student space; the Faculty Senate endorses it in April, but Dean Joshua Vossler's position is that staffing makes it unworkable.

patterns.name: Technology
patterns.what_it_is: Whatever the university has not yet bought students. The subject changes completely every decade; the posture does not.
patterns.how_it_changed: Cable TV in dorm rooms (1983) gives way to photocopiers and student email accounts and a Technology Committee (1996), then typewriters for the library in the same season (1997), then a printing quota study (2006), a campus-wide wireless network paid for by a $45 fee (2006), a $1,995 streaming-video subscription Drew Eclov called 'a version of YouTube for higher education' (2007), iPads (2011), charging stations (2013), recycled computers (2020), graphing calculators (2024), and finally bulk AI subscriptions (2026). The consistent move is SGA buying, on a small scale, the device gap it can see.

instances.what: ASG asks for cable television in dormitory rooms.
The September 17 meeting creates the SGA Technology Committee and discusses intramural facilities, photocopiers in dorms and Campus Clean Up; student email accounts recur through the fall minutes.
A bill to buy typewriters for the library, the same week as designated driver cards; the year's legislation also covers student e-mail addresses in the directory.
Bill 99-10-F creates the SGA position of Information Technology Director, with a companion bill amending the constitution to include website guidelines.

Resolution 08-06-F backs a university study of a computer-lab printing quota after administrators told the Student Affairs committee how many pages some students were printing. In February SGA takes up a $45-per-semester fee to pay for a campus-wide wireless network, a health centre and Ivan Wilson renovations.
The Academic Affairs Committee prepares legislation for a roughly $1,995 United Streaming subscription — about 45,000 educational video clips.
SGA and WKU Libraries buy five KwikBoost charging stations for $1,598, with two going to the Glasgow and Owensboro campuses.

Bill 2923-S creates Borrow-a-Calculator after a survey found 17 percent of students surveyed owned no calculator and 93 percent had taken a class requiring one; 28 are borrowed that semester and five more bought in October.

Chief Communications Officer Preston Jenkins reports WKU's new Artificial Intelligence Committee is in early talks about bulk subscriptions to AI products such as ChatGPT Pro for all students and a possible introductory AI course for freshmen.

patterns.name: Mental health, health services and student wellbeing
patterns.what_it_is: The campus clinic, insurance, vaccination, sexual assault prevention, suicide prevention, counselling.
patterns.span: 1989-2026 (37 years; nothing in the archive before 1989)
patterns.how_it_changed: It enters the record as a single resolution asking for education about a disease — Resolution 89-3-F on AIDS, HIV and STDs — and as defence of the campus clinic (a joint mailing to parents in 1991, letters to Ransdell in 1999, the clinic taken back in-house in 2001 when its contractor went out of business). From 2016 it becomes structural: a standing SAVES committee, then a constitutionally defined Student Mental Health and Wellbeing Committee, then a required semesterly meeting with the Counseling Center director and Title IX coordinator, then in 2025-26 a full-year programme with its own campus data — 44 percent of WKU students reporting depression symptoms, 10 percent having considered suicide in the past year — and a proposed advisory board to advise upper administration.

instances.what: Resolution 89-3-F: ASG corresponds with administrators requesting education on AIDS, HIV and sexually transmitted diseases.
Falmlen opens the year with student health at the top of her agenda; in December the Residence Hall Association and ASG send a joint mailing asking parents to support the campus health service.

Vice president Matthew Bastin writes to president Gary Ransdell expressing SGA's concerns about student health services, closing the year by taking a student welfare issue to the top of the administration.

Resolution 6-15-F unanimously supports requiring meningococcal meningitis vaccination for incoming freshmen in on-campus housing from the class of 2020; Ransdell declines in March 2016, citing a $143.77 cost for uninsured students at the Graves-Gilbert Clinic and saying WKU will 'stop short of requiring it.'

The senate creates SAVES — Standing Against Violence and Ending Self-harm — to work on sexual assault prevention, suicide prevention and expanded mental health resources with the Counseling and Testing Center.

Resolution 1-17-F passes 29-1 supporting a one-credit-hour sexual assault education course in the Colonnade, its author noting a student could pass four years at WKU without any sexual assault training.

Bill 22-22-S amends the constitution to redefine the Student Mental Health and Wellbeing Committee's duties; Bill 6-22-S requires a committee chair or delegate to meet the Counseling Center director and Title IX coordinator at least once a semester.

Resolution 2-23-S unanimously supports placing Narcan in WKU residence halls; SGA had budgeted about $1,000 before a UK harm reduction specialist secured the product on a government grant, and Housing plans AED-style boxes across its 15 dorms by August 1.
Resolution 4-25-S supports a Mental Health and Suicide Prevention Advisory Board; co-author Emma Harris says Counseling Center staffing shortages have pushed students to rely on resident advisors.

A year-long push closes with an Out of Darkness walk on April 18, built on Jay Gabbard's data that 44 percent of WKU students report depression symptoms and 10 percent considered suicide in the past year; recommendations including moving counselling out of Potter Hall go through the Counseling Center Review Committee.

patterns.name: Sustainability, recycling and the campus environment
patterns.what_it_is: Paper drives, bins, cleanups, then buildings, food and a dedicated fee.
patterns.span: 1973-2026 (53 years, with a long documented gap)
patterns.how_it_changed: It is a scrappy volunteer effort in the 1970s — a paper-recycling programme the city's own ordinance leaves ASG 'holding the bag' on, and by 1974 a Herald reporter finds ASG ecology projects 'non-existent.' It returns in the early 1990s as budgeted money, recycling bins, Adopt-a-Spot and Earth Day. From 2015 it becomes institutional: a committee created by executive proposal, made permanent by constitutional amendment in 2016, then a demand that every new campus building meet LEED standards (29-0, 2018), and finally SGA proposing a $5-per-semester fee on students to fund the Office of Sustainability (2024) — the same office whose food pantry SGA now restocks.

instances.what: ASG sponsors a book exchange and fights a city recycling ordinance that left it holding the bag on trash collection for its paper-recycling programme; that autumn a push for paper recycling sits alongside the housing survey.
Janet Steen reports in the Herald that ASG ecology projects are non-existent, in the same issue as protesters urging a revamping of the organisation.
ASG budgets more money for environmental efforts in the first week of the fall semester; a recycling resolution has its first reading that September.
The final full meeting of the year takes up Adopt-a-Spot and Earth Day alongside the budget, elections and a one-card ID system.
An executive proposal creating a sustainability committee passes unanimously.

Resolution 3-16-S supports recycling in the DSU, Garrett and Tower food courts; in November the Sustainability committee is made permanent under the constitution and a resolution passes to remove styrofoam from WKU dining. A sustainability clause seeking a zero-emissions campus is softened to raising WKU's AASHE STARS rating.
Resolution 8-18-F, requiring all new campus buildings to meet LEED standards, passes 29-0.
Senators unanimously fund a community garden outside the Office of Sustainability.
$570.02 for an e-waste recycling bin on main campus.

Resolution 26-23-S puts SGA behind a $5-per-semester sustainability fee with proceeds to the Office of Sustainability, alongside Bill 25-23-S giving that office $500 for the food pantry, scholarships and an Earth Day event.

patterns.name: Dining, food service and food insecurity
patterns.what_it_is: Hours, menus, contracts, and — recently — whether students can afford to eat.
patterns.how_it_changed: For twenty years it is convenience: microwaves in the cafeterias (1990), food court hours (1997), two weeks' notice of service changes (2003), a South Campus food court, 24-hour dining pushed by a student petition with 700 signatures in a week (2013), vegetarian options (2016). Then in 2018 the object changes from the food to the contract — a unanimous resolution against a 20-year Aramark deal escalating the non-meal-plan dining fee from $75 to $150 to $300 to $350, about $2,800 over four years, which Dahmer says was never brought to SGA or the full Board of Regents. From 2022 the frame is hunger: swipe donation programmes, a food-insecurity clause added to course syllabi, and a food pantry bill amended from $123 to $750 in response to SNAP cuts.

instances.what: Bill #90-4-F requests microwaves in campus cafeterias.
Outgoing SGA correspondence to the administration covers food court hours alongside ice machines and campus safety.
SGA unanimously passes legislation calling on Dining Services to post and advertise changes to service hours or facilities at least two weeks before they take effect.

A 24-hour dining resolution gets its first read after McCormack Hall RA Nick Conrad gathers more than 700 signatures in about a week; by 2014 Einstein's Bagels is under consideration for a 24-hour study area.
Resolution 5-16-S supports vegetarian options on the DSU meal plan.

Resolution 3-18-S passes unanimously supporting renegotiation of the 20-year Aramark contract, under which the per-semester dining fee for full-time students without a meal plan would climb $75 to $150 to $300 to $350 — about $2,800 over four years.

Craighead raises long DSU food lines, partly attributed to a lack of employment; a 'Vet Our Vendors' bill passes 16-0 asking WKU to codify a dining-vendor vetting process after a Lost River Pizza social media post.

A meal swipe donation programme lets students donate excess swipes in weeks 4, 8 and 12, with the WKU Restaurant Group matching one for every four; Resolution 10-22-S adds a food insecurity clause to course syllabi.

Swipe it Forward lets students donate up to three swipes a semester; a food pantry bill introduced at $123 is amended up to $750 after SNAP cuts, its sponsor handing out 24 slips of paper, six marked with a star, to show that one in four people aged 18 to 26 experience hunger during the year.

WKU Restaurant Group representatives field questions on Steak 'n Shake seasoning, Subway kiosks and spicy chicken sandwiches on Chick-fil-A's meal-swipe menu, and report about 60,000 meal transactions a week.

patterns.name: Evaluating the teaching
patterns.what_it_is: Student evaluation of faculty, courses, teaching assistants and advisors — repeatedly won, repeatedly lost, repeatedly restarted.
patterns.how_it_changed: The first attempt is in 1969, an ASG committee compiling Western's first student teacher-evaluation effort while the Herald editorialises demanding the tabulation move faster. Every generation since has fought the same two-stage battle: get the evaluation done, then get the results published. ASG runs 'the best course evaluation yet' (1972), pushes teacher evaluations (1978) and is told by the Herald to make them public (1979), considers making them required (1987), tries to find a way to print them (1989), wins a mandatory published evaluation on paper with Resolution 00-2-S (2000), then scales it back to five questions posted on TopNet (2004), then extends it to teaching assistants (2013, approved by a Board of Regents committee) and finally to academic advisors (2021).

instances.what: An ASG committee compiles the results of Western's first student teacher-evaluation effort; the Herald had already editorialised demanding the tabulation move faster.
The Herald judges ASG's course evaluation 'the best yet' as filing opens for fall offices.
The Herald editorialises that ASG should make its teacher evaluation public.
Associated Student Government takes up a proposal to make course evaluations a requirement.

Resolution 00-2-S, by Amanda Coates and Adam Howard, asks the Faculty Senate to approve a mandatory SGA-sponsored faculty evaluation published from fall 2000, with a questionnaire asking whether an instructor takes attendance, offers extra credit or gives comprehensive finals; Coates says SGA did not want the tool 'at the expense of unnecessarily upsetting faculty.'

A two-year pilot proposes adding five questions on office hours, punctuality and textbook use to faculty evaluations and posting the answers on TopNet, after SGA scaled back the earlier push to release entire evaluations.
The teaching assistant evaluation resolution clears the senate and is unanimously approved by a Board of Regents committee; Dodds says the idea had been worked on for many years.
Resolution 1.21f, addressing the lack of an advisor evaluation system, passes 21-2 as the first resolution of the 21st Senate.

patterns.name: Voter registration and getting students to the polls
patterns.what_it_is: SGA turning outward to state and national elections, as opposed to worrying about its own.
patterns.how_it_changed: It begins as a table: a voter registration drive restarted in 1991, running through the 1992 and 1996 fall agendas alongside the budget and the bonfire. In the 2000s it becomes a resolution — the senate suspending its own bylaws so it could urge students to vote before November 4 arrived — and a mock election with the Secretary of State that drew 127 votes. In 2018 it becomes a demand on the university: cancel classes on election day, backed by the figure that of 290,000 Kentucky students registered in 2016 only about 13 percent voted. By the 2020s the ask is infrastructural — a trolley to State Street polling places, then a polling centre on campus itself, with an SGA president who chairs the Hilltoppers Vote Coalition.

instances.what: Officers attend a Bowling Green city meeting to press the noise ordinance fight, and the organisation restarts its voter registration drive.
The first meeting of the fall discusses a new logo, student discount cards, a voter registration drive and committee assignments.
A September meeting takes up a voter registration drive alongside Provide-A-Ride, roller blading rules, a bonfire and student email accounts.

SGA unanimously passes a resolution recommending students vote in the November 4 state election and research candidates' stands on higher education, suspending the bylaws so it could pass before the vote.
SGA co-sponsors a mock gubernatorial election with the Secretary of State's office at Centennial Mall; 127 students vote, choosing Steve Beshear over Ernie Fletcher 74 to 50.

Resolution 5-18-F unanimously asks WKU to cancel classes on November 6 so students can get to the polls, with $300 to the Reg 2 Vote campaign; Francis Wilson tells senators that of 290,000 Kentucky students registered in 2016, only about 13 percent voted.
Caboni tells the senate WKU will use the Historic Railpark's BG Trolley to carry students to State Street polling places on a class day.
Vice President Donte Reed tells the senate he is working with a student advocacy group to get a polling centre on campus, saying he otherwise has to drive about three hours home to vote.
Caden Lucas, chairman of the Hilltoppers Vote Coalition, is elected president; the coalition is among the 33 groups sharing $10,000 in organizational aid that March.

patterns.name: Its own constitution
patterns.what_it_is: Rewriting, amending and re-codifying the governing documents. The most reliably recurring internal activity in the entire sixty years.
patterns.how_it_changed: The early rewrites are about legitimacy — a new constitution sent back for study (1969), four amendments to referendum (1970), a section-by-section vote with the full text printed in the Herald (1972), the whole thing consolidated into a single document after twenty years of patching (1986). The 2004 Constitutional Convention is the hinge: three branches, and the quietest and most consequential clause, that every enrolled student became a member of SGA with the right to vote in its elections. After that the amendments track who is missing from the room — college seats replacing class seats and guaranteed regional-campus seats (2013), an international student seat (2013), first-generation (2019), Mahurin Honors College (2023). The 2025 amendment goes the other way, renaming the DEI Committee the Action and Opportunity Committee after a federal executive order, ratified by 88 percent of voters.

instances.what: The Associated Student Government returns its proposed new constitution for further study while limiting how long the review could run.
Congress votes section by section on a rewritten constitution, the Herald printing the full text of the proposed executive branch; a 'Vote Yes' campaign precedes the two-day referendum in March.
'The constitution of the WKU Associated Students with amendments' — the only surviving snapshot of how the 1966 framework had been patched over two decades.
The body votes on 7 April to rename itself the Student Government Association; students ratify it by referendum on 14 April; it takes effect that autumn.

The Constitutional Convention creates the Executive Cabinet, Senate and Judicial Council — and makes every enrolled student a member of SGA with the right to vote in its elections. Only 132 of about 18,000 students vote on it.

A package of amendments replaces class-year senate seats with college-based representation and guarantees seats for regional campuses such as Glasgow and Owensboro; the bylaw barring SGA members from SGA-sponsored scholarships is stripped out and fails.

Students ratify all six referendums, making SAVES, MyCampusToo and Sustainability permanent committees, lowering the GPA requirement to 2.0, creating regional campus ambassadors and requiring more accessible executive discretionary spending reports.

Three Legislative Operations bills correct references to a 'University Senate' that had since split into separate Faculty and Staff senates, reconcile bylaws on expelling senators with a constitution that only provides for impeachment, and update committee names that had drifted.

Bill 21-25-S restructures the DEI Committee as the Action and Opportunity Committee after Trump's executive order; senators phone absent members onto Zoom to reach quorum, and students ratify it with 88 percent.
The Senate adopts a fully codified rewrite of its Executive and Legislative Bylaws, superseding all prior versions.

patterns.name: Turnout, apathy and the annual report card
patterns.what_it_is: The organisation's permanent anxiety about whether anyone is paying attention, and the Herald's permanent willingness to say they are not.
patterns.how_it_changed: Almost nothing changes except the vocabulary. The 1966 ratification drew 2,538 votes — 'a larger raw turnout than most SGA elections have managed since.' The 1968 election drew 2,894, about 34 percent of an 8,500-student enrollment, and the same issue carried an editorial headed 'Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference.' Sixty years later the highest turnout on record is 2,442 in 2016, against an enrollment several times larger. The only thing the record actually establishes as a cause is competition: in 2026, turnout jumped 66 percent to 1,601 in the first genuinely contested presidential race in years. The Herald's tone moved from scolding non-voters (1967) to explaining them (a 1979 piece justifying student apathy in ASG voting) to simply printing the number.

instances.what: The constitution is ratified 1,812 to 726 on a four-day referendum; 2,538 students voted. That October the Herald judges leaders are performing well but failing to communicate with the students they represent.
Straeffer beats Whitley 1,732 to 1,098; total turnout 2,894, about 34 percent of roughly 8,500 students. The same issue: 'Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference.'
With filing open, the Herald reports twenty student government offices going begging for candidates; by election eve the field has filled to 84.
'Bruce Smith, Christy Vogt Survive as 527 Cast Ballots.'
The spring primary draws 830 voters; the same issue carries a piece justifying student apathy in ASG voting — the paper had moved from scolding non-voters to explaining them.
The Herald runs an article arguing apathy is killing both Associated Student Government and the Residence Hall Association.
Anti-Apathy Week draws enough criticism that President Amos Gott has to defend it in print; that April, candidate withdrawals save a primary that would otherwise have been invalid.
Coates and Martin win by three votes on a recount, 614-611; total turnout 1,436.
A Herald editorial faults students after only 132 of about 18,000 voted on SGA's new constitution, contrasting it with the 86 percent who voted in South Africa's 1999 general elections.
Spring turnout falls to 908, down 555 votes from the previous year; the editorial calls turnout below 1,000 pathetic.
Richey is re-elected with 2,442 voters, one of the highest-turnout elections in the association's history.
Kurtz announces POLLapalooza with a goal of 3,000 voters; the April election draws 966.
1,601 students vote, 635 more than the year before — a 66 percent jump in the first contested presidential race in three years.

patterns.name: Race, representation and who gets a seat
patterns.what_it_is: Not on the brief's list, but one of the deepest recurrences in the file: who is in the room, whose name is on the building, and whether SGA speaks for anyone outside itself.
patterns.how_it_changed: It starts with individual fights the archive records mostly as headlines — a resolution deploring a cheerleader ruling (1972), rejecting Dero Downing's position on an Office of Black Affairs (1972), a discrimination resolution failing with fourteen members abstaining (1977), a Minorities Board established (1979). WKU's student regent seat integrated the Board of Regents first, in 1974, seven years before the first Black gubernatorial appointee. From the mid-1990s the mechanism shifts to policy — anti-discrimination language, the Campus Pride Index, a transgender resolution passed 18-5 at the last meeting of 2012 — and from 2013 to structural seats: an international student senator, first-generation, ISEC, Honors. The 2016-17 peak (the Jonesville scholarship, Resolution 6-17-S on reparations, 19-10-1) draws national coverage and a flat rejection from Ransdell. The last decade also carries the internal cost: the harassment Andi Dahmer described and litigated, the Alpha Xi Delta veto, and repeated Herald reporting that 40 percent of SGA seats belong to Greek members against under 8 percent of the student body.

instances.what: An ASG resolution deplores a cheerleader ruling as the university bows to Black students' demands after a bitter squabble over squad selection; that September ASG rejects President Dero Downing's position on an Office of Black Affairs.
Gregory McKinney is sworn in as WKU's first African American student regent — seven years before Julius Price became the first Black gubernatorial appointee to the board.
Fourteen members abstain as ASG rejects a resolution on discrimination.
ASG establishes a Minorities Board, following the previous fall's push to add minority voices to the presidential screening panel.
SGA passes a measure calling for gays to be included in Western's anti-discrimination policy by a slim margin.
The Herald reports 21 of SGA's 50 members belong to Greek organisations, more than 40 percent, against less than 8 percent of the student body; two fraternities account for nine of them.
At the last meeting of the year the senate passes a transgender and gender-nonconforming support resolution 18-5, with students who were not SGA members attending specifically to watch the vote.
A referendum creates a Navitas/ESL international student senate seat with 310 of 426 votes — Boka says it would make WKU the first student government in the state with an international senate seat.

The senate creates the Jonesville Memorial Scholarship, allocating $750 for the Black community WKU bought and displaced in the late 1960s for under $200,000; Dillon McCormick calls it 'a kind of symbolic gesture to atone for the wrong that we did.'

Resolution 6-17-S, by Andrea Ambam and Brian Anderson, supporting reparations for Black students, passes 19-10-1 and draws national wire coverage; Ransdell states within days that it is not a university position.
Resolution 4-19-F seeking discipline against Alpha Xi Delta after a video of members singing a racial slur passes 24-7, then is vetoed 4-0 by the executive board and the veto sustained.

Legislation offers SGA's support to WKU's Naming and Symbols Task Force in renaming buildings tied to racism; Northeast Hall is renamed for Margaret Munday, WKU's first African American student to enrol, the first building on campus named after an African American.

The advocacy group 'For the People' tells the senate SGA was the only major organisation not to oppose Turning Point USA bringing Kyle Rittenhouse to campus, and says 40 percent of the Senate belongs to Greek life.

notes:
FILE READ IN FULL: all 61 year records in /Users/samkurtz/Downloads/sga60/data/years.json (1966-67 through 2026-27), including every leader note and profile, every event, and the organization/documents blocks. Every instance above is drawn from that file only.

WHERE THE ARCHIVE IS THIN — these gaps are findings, not omissions:

1. The 1960s and 1970s are almost entirely an election-and-governance record. Coverage in those decades is dominated by presidential races, turnout, the student regent seat and constitutional revision. There is no campus lighting item before 1985, no emergency-phone item before 1993, no library-hours item before 1986, no mental-health item before 1989, no technology item before 1983 (cable TV). It is not clear whether SGA was not doing this work or whether only the Herald headline index survives for those years — many 1960s-70s entries are explicitly headline-only, e.g. 1968's 'Menser Discusses Head Fee' and 'Past Performance of Associated Student Government Analyzed' where "the archive does not yet hold the text of either article, only their headlines."

2. Whole years are near-blank. 1979-80 (James Hargroave / Jamie Hargrove) states outright: "The archive does not yet show what Hargrove's administration passed or fought over during 1979-80." 1969-70's Zielke entry says "What the Zielke-Porter administration did in office beyond the year-opening outline is not yet confirmed." The published result of the April 1987 presidential election is not recorded at all — the plaque carries Todd through 1988 on a two-year plate and the surviving indexed issues do not record who won.

3. Sustainability has a documented seventeen-year hole: paper recycling and ecology in 1973-74, then nothing until the 1991 recycling resolution.

4. The 1990s preserve legislation better than personnel: several years' organization blocks say "no full senate officer list, committee structure, or seat count survives beyond the president." Conversely 1993-94 preserves at least seventeen numbered resolutions from a single semester (93-4-F through 93-20-F), described as "the fullest single-semester record in the collection."

5. 2002-03 is partly inaccessible: "TopSCHOLAR's full-text PDFs for this year sit behind an automated-access check and have not been read."

6. Several outcomes are never resolved in the record: the 1991 FBI/IRS investigation of regents chair Joe Iracane ("No source found reports the investigation's outcome"); the 1999 investigation into racially charged campaign fliers ("No source found reports how, or whether, the investigation was resolved"); the 1979 activities-funding fight; the 1972 Kentucky Civil Liberties Union lawsuit connected to Associated Students and The Fly.

TWO THINGS I DELIBERATELY DID NOT FLATTEN:
- Campus safety before ~1993 in this archive is about dorm rules and supervision, not lighting and phones. Treating them as one continuous "safety" thread would be smoothing; they are different asks with different targets.
- "Organisational aid" as a named budget line only appears from the mid-2000s. Earlier money-to-clubs activity exists (1996: "SGA giving more money to campus clubs") but is not the same instrument.

STRUCTURAL FACT UNDERPINNING SEVERAL PATTERNS: the student regent seat was created by 1968 state legislation, carried no vote for at least four years, and was a separately elected office until it merged with the presidency — the archive shows Falmlen holding both in 1991, and by the 2000s the offices are automatically merged. This is why the same person now writes the resolution against a fee and then votes on it, and why the 2009 Boles resignation left students without a voting voice on the board for 26 days.
